Drawing/PE.body: The elements of art are the building blocks of every drawing: line, shape, form, colour, texture and space. A line leads the eye; shapes are flat (circle, square); forms are three-dimensional (cube, sphere); texture is how a surface looks or feels; space is the area around and between things. In a test, a question may ask which element is missing from a picture, or what makes a flat drawing look deep — the answer is usually shading and perspective. Roman Urdu: drawing ke bunyadi ajzaa — lakeer, shakal, rang, banawat aur jagah. Recall first: cover this note and list the six elements of art from memory.
Drawing/PE.title: Drawing Basics — The Elements of Art

Drawing/PE.body: Primary colours are red, blue and yellow — they cannot be made by mixing other colours. Secondary colours are made by mixing two primaries: red + yellow = orange, blue + yellow = green, red + blue = purple. Warm colours (red, orange, yellow) feel lively and near; cool colours (blue, green, purple) feel calm and far. Artists use warm colours to bring things forward and cool colours to push them back. Black, white and grey are neutral colours. Recall first: cover this note and name the three primary colours and the three secondary colours they make.
Drawing/PE.title: Colour Theory — Primary and Secondary Colours

Drawing/PE.body: Physical fitness has five main components: strength (how much force muscles can produce), endurance (how long you can keep going), flexibility (how far joints can move), speed (how fast you can move) and body composition. A PE teacher trains all of them, not just one — a runner needs endurance and speed, a gymnast needs flexibility and strength. Warm-up before exercise and cool-down after it prevent injuries. Roman Urdu: taqat, bardasht, lachak, raftaar — ye paanchon fitness ke hisse hain. Recall first: cover this note and list the five components of physical fitness.
Drawing/PE.title: Physical Education — Components of Fitness

Drawing/PE.body: Team sizes are a favourite MCQ topic. Cricket: 11 players per side. Football (soccer): 11 players per side. Hockey: 11 players per side. Badminton: 1 player in singles, 2 in doubles. Volleyball: 6 players per side on court. A game also has its field or court name: cricket is played on a pitch/ground, football on a field, hockey on a field or astroturf, badminton on a court. Learn the number with the game together, not alone — 'cricket-11, football-11, hockey-11'. Recall first: cover this note and say how many players each side has in cricket, football, hockey and volleyball.
Drawing/PE.title: Common Games — Players Per Side
Hockey — The Basics
Drawing/PE.body: Field hockey is played by two teams of 11 players, using curved sticks to hit a small hard ball into the other team's goal. A standard match lasts 60 minutes, played as four quarters of 15 minutes each. Modern hockey is usually played on astroturf, a smooth artificial surface that keeps the ball rolling fast and true. Only the flat side of the stick may be used to play the ball. Roman Urdu: hockey mein 11 khilari, 60 minute ka match aur 4 quarter hote hain. Recall first: cover this note and say how many players, how many minutes and how many quarters a hockey match has.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Physical Education Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — PET: Physical Education section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: Racket Games — Tennis, Badminton and Table Tennis
Drawing/PE.body: Tennis points are counted 15, 30, 40, then game; singles has one player per side and doubles has two. Badminton uses rally scoring to 21 points, with a shuttlecock (also called a birdie) hit over a net. Table tennis games go to 11 points with a lead of 2, played with small bats and a light ball on a table divided by a net. All three games reward quick feet, a strong wrist and sharp eyes. Roman Urdu: tennis mein 15, 30, 40; badminton 21 aur table tennis 11 points ka game hota hai. Recall first: cover this note and give the winning score for badminton and table tennis.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Physical Education Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — PET: Physical Education section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: Volleyball and Basketball — Court Measurements
Drawing/PE.body: Volleyball is played by two teams of 6 on a court divided by a high net — 2.43 metres for men and 2.24 metres for women. Players hit the ball over the net without letting it touch their own floor. Basketball has 5 players per side, aiming at a hoop whose rim is 10 feet (3.05 metres) above the floor. Both games need jumping, quick passes and teamwork. Roman Urdu: volleyball mein 6 khilari aur uncha jaal; basketball mein 5 khilari aur 10 foot uncha hoop hota hai. Recall first: cover this note and give the men's volleyball net height and the basketball hoop height.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Physical Education Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — PET: Physical Education section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: Cricket — Overs, Wickets and Formats
Drawing/PE.body: Cricket is played by two teams of 11. One over has 6 legal balls, and a wicket has 3 stumps with 2 bails on top. In One Day Internationals each side faces a maximum of 50 overs; in Twenty20 matches each side faces 20 overs. The batting side scores runs while the fielding side tries to take wickets. Test matches have no over limit and can last up to five days. Roman Urdu: aik over mein 6 gendain, wicket mein 3 stump; ODI 50 aur T20 20 overs ka hota hai. Recall first: cover this note and say how many balls in an over, stumps in a wicket and overs in an ODI.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Physical Education Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — PET: Physical Education section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: Football — Key Rules
Drawing/PE.body: Football is played by two teams of 11, including one goalkeeper each, over 90 minutes (two halves of 45). Only the goalkeeper may handle the ball, and only inside the team's own penalty area. A penalty kick is taken from 12 yards (11 metres) out. A yellow card is a warning; a red card sends the player off for the rest of the match. The team that scores more goals wins. Roman Urdu: football mein 11 khilari, 90 minute; laal card par khilari bahar ho jata hai. Recall first: cover this note and say the match length, the penalty distance and what a red card means.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Physical Education Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — PET: Physical Education section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: Athletics — Track and Field Events
Drawing/PE.body: Athletics has track events (running) and field events (jumping and throwing). A standard track lap is 400 metres; sprints include the 100 m and 200 m. In relays, four runners each run a leg and pass a baton. Field events include the long jump and high jump, and the throws: shot put (heavy metal ball), discus, javelin (spear) and hammer. The farthest legal jump or throw wins. Roman Urdu: track par dor, field mein chhalang aur phainkna hota hai; aik lap 400 metre ka hota hai. Recall first: cover this note and name two track and two field events.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Physical Education Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — PET: Physical Education section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: The Body in Sport — Bones, Muscles and Heart
Drawing/PE.body: An adult skeleton has 206 bones. The femur (thigh bone) is the longest and strongest; the stapes in the ear is the smallest. The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle. The heart pumps blood around the body; a resting adult heart beats about 60 to 100 times per minute, and the pulse is easiest to feel at the wrist. Regular exercise makes the heart stronger and the bones denser. Roman Urdu: jism mein 206 haddiyan; femur sab se lambi aur stapes sab se chhoti haddi hai. Recall first: cover this note and name the longest bone, the smallest bone and the normal resting heart rate.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Physical Education Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — PET: Physical Education section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: Food for Sport — Energy and Repair
Drawing/PE.body: Food is fuel and repair material. Carbohydrates (bread, rice, pasta) are the body's main energy source. Protein (meat, eggs, lentils, milk) builds and repairs muscles after training. Fats store energy, and water replaces what sweat removes — drink before, during and after exercise. A balanced diet mixes all food groups. Body Mass Index (BMI) relates weight to height and is used as a general guide to healthy weight. Roman Urdu: carbohydrate taqat deta hai, protein pathon ki marammat karta hai. Recall first: cover this note and say which nutrient gives energy and which repairs muscles.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Physical Education Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — PET: Physical Education section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: First Aid on the Field — RICE and Prevention
Drawing/PE.body: For a sprain or bruise, remember RICE: Rest the injured part, Ice it to reduce swelling, Compress it with a bandage, and Elevate it above the heart. Warming up prepares muscles for work and cooling down lets the heart rate fall slowly — both cut the risk of injury. Stop playing if pain is sharp or sudden, drink water, and tell a teacher or coach about any injury at once. Roman Urdu: chot par RICE — araam, barf, patti aur uncha rakhna. Recall first: cover this note and expand RICE.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Physical Education Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — PET: Physical Education section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: Sports Bodies and the Olympic Games
Drawing/PE.body: World sport is run by federations: FIFA governs football, the ICC governs cricket and the IOC (International Olympic Committee) runs the Olympic Games. The Olympic Games are held every four years; the Olympic flag shows five interlocking rings, standing for the inhabited continents of the world. The Games celebrate fair play — playing by the rules, respecting opponents and officials, and winning or losing with grace. Roman Urdu: FIFA football, ICC cricket aur IOC Olympics chalati hai; paanch halqe paanch bara-e-azam ki nishani hain. Recall first: cover this note and match FIFA, ICC and IOC to their sports.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Physical Education Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — PET: Physical Education section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: Line, Shape and Form — The Building Blocks
Drawing/PE.body: Line is the first tool of drawing. Vertical lines stand up, horizontal lines lie across, diagonal lines slant, and curved lines bend. A contour line follows the edge of an object. Lines also carry weight: a pressed line looks heavy and near, while a light line looks far away. Shapes are flat — circles, squares and triangles have only length and width. Forms have depth as well: a circle becomes a sphere, a square becomes a cube, a rectangle becomes a cylinder, and a triangle becomes a cone. Shading is what turns a flat shape into a form the eye believes. Roman Urdu: lakeer, shakal aur form — shakal chapti hoti hai, form mein gehrai hoti hai. Recall first: cover this note and name the four line directions and the four basic solid forms.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Drawing Fundamentals Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — DM: Drawing section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: Value and Shading — Light, Shadow and Tone
Drawing/PE.body: Value is how light or dark a tone is. A value scale runs from white, through pale grey, middle grey and dark grey, to black. On a lit object, the highlight is the lightest spot, where light strikes first. Next comes the light side, then the mid-tone, then the core shadow on the darkest side, and the cast shadow the object throws onto the surface. A little reflected light often lifts the edge of the shadow side. A smooth gradient moves slowly from light to dark with no hard steps. Roman Urdu: value ka matlab hai rang ka halka ya gehra hona; highlight sab se roshan jagah hai. Recall first: cover this note and list the parts of a shaded object in order from lightest to darkest.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Drawing Fundamentals Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — DM: Drawing section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: Perspective — One Point, Two Points and Eye Level
Drawing/PE.body: Perspective makes flat drawings look deep. The horizon line sits at the viewer's eye level. In one-point perspective, parallel lines run to a single vanishing point — the view down a straight road or corridor. In two-point perspective, there are two vanishing points, one on each side — the corner of a building. Objects nearer the viewer look larger and lower on the page; objects farther away look smaller and closer to the horizon. Foreshortening is when an object pointing towards the viewer looks shorter than it really is. Roman Urdu: horizon line aankh ki satah par hoti hai; aik nuqta nazar se seedhi sarrak, do nuqton se imarat ka kona banta hai. Recall first: cover this note and say when to use one-point and when to use two-point perspective.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Drawing Fundamentals Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — DM: Drawing section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: The Colour Wheel — Analogous, Neutral and Monochrome
Drawing/PE.body: The colour wheel runs red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, and back to red. Analogous colours sit next to each other, such as blue, blue-green and green, and give calm harmony. Neutral colours — black, white, grey and brown — sit outside the wheel and soften bright colours. A monochromatic scheme uses one colour only, varied with tints and shades. Tertiary colours mix a primary with the secondary beside it, such as red-orange and blue-green. Hue is the name of a colour; intensity is how bright or dull it looks. Roman Urdu: colour wheel mein rang tarteeb se hote hain; qareebi rang, neutral rang aur aik hi rang ki scheme is se banti hai. Recall first: cover this note and give one example each of analogous, neutral and monochromatic colour.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Drawing Fundamentals Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — DM: Drawing section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: Geometric Construction — Compass, Bisectors and Angles
Drawing/PE.body: Geometric construction uses only a compass and a straightedge. A compass draws circles and arcs of a set radius — the distance from the centre to the edge; the diameter is twice the radius. To bisect a line, draw arcs of equal radius from each end and join where they cross; the crossing line cuts the first line into two equal halves. The same method bisects an angle: bisecting 90 degrees gives 45 degrees. A 60-degree angle comes from an equilateral triangle, whose three sides and three angles are equal. Parallel lines can be drawn with two set squares sliding against each other. Roman Urdu: compass se daira banta hai; bisect ka matlab hai do barabar hisse karna. Recall first: cover this note and describe how to bisect a line and what bisecting 90 degrees gives.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Drawing Fundamentals Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — DM: Drawing section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: Drawing Tools and Materials — Pencils, Erasers and Boards
Drawing/PE.body: Pencils are graded by hardness: H pencils are hard and light, B pencils are soft and dark, and HB sits in the middle. A 2H suits light construction lines; a 6B gives deep dark tones. A kneaded eraser is soft and mouldable: it lifts graphite gently and can be shaped to a point. A blending stump (tortillon) smooths pencil tone. Set squares give exact 90-45-45 and 90-60-30 triangles; a T-square draws horizontals across a drawing board, and a protractor measures angles. Cartridge paper is the usual drawing paper. Charcoal, pastels and crayons are dry media; a light spray of fixative stops them smudging. Roman Urdu: H pencil halki, B pencil gehri lakeer deti hai; kneaded eraser naram hota hai. Recall first: cover this note and say which pencil suits construction lines and which tool blends tone.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Drawing Fundamentals Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — DM: Drawing section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: Composition — Foreground, Balance and Focus
Drawing/PE.body: Composition is how parts of a drawing are arranged. The foreground is nearest the viewer, the middle ground sits in the centre, and the background is farthest away. The focal point is the part the eye meets first — it is often placed off-centre. The rule of thirds divides the page into nine equal boxes with two vertical and two horizontal lines; placing key parts on those lines or their crossings makes a lively arrangement. Balance can be symmetrical, with both sides alike, or asymmetrical, with unlike parts balanced by weight and tone. Overlapping shapes show depth: the shape in front hides part of the shape behind. Roman Urdu: foreground qareeb, background door hota hai; focal point woh jagah hai jahan nazar pehle jati hai. Recall first: cover this note and explain the rule of thirds in one line.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Drawing Fundamentals Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — DM: Drawing section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: Drawing from Observation — Sighting, Grids and Negative Space
Drawing/PE.body: Drawing from observation means drawing what the eye sees, not what the mind expects. Sighting is measuring with a pencil held at arm's length: close one eye, line the pencil up with the object, and compare heights and widths. The grid method divides both the reference and the paper into equal squares, so each small part can be copied square by square — it also enlarges or reduces a picture. Negative space is the empty area around and between objects; drawing it often fixes a shape that looks wrong. A gesture drawing is a fast, loose sketch that catches movement and pose before detail is added. Roman Urdu: mashahidah se drawing mein pencil se naapna, grid ka tareeqa aur khaali jagah kaam aati hai. Recall first: cover this note and say what sighting, the grid method and negative space each do.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Drawing Fundamentals Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — DM: Drawing section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: The Human Figure — Proportion in Heads
Drawing/PE.body: Figure drawing measures the body in heads. The head is the unit: an adult figure is commonly drawn about seven and a half heads tall. The chin sits at one head, the waist at about three, and the knees below the halfway mark. Children are drawn with larger heads relative to their height — a small child may be only four or five heads tall. Proportion means the parts relate correctly to each other; a head drawn too large makes the whole figure look childlike. Roman Urdu: insani jism ko sar ke hisaab se naapa jata hai; bara aadmi taqreeban saadhay saat sar lamba hota hai. Recall first: cover this note and say how many heads tall an adult figure is commonly drawn.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Drawing Fundamentals Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — DM: Drawing section (20)

Drawing/PE.title: Shading Techniques — Hatching, Stippling and Blending
Drawing/PE.body: Hatching shades with parallel lines; the closer the lines, the darker the tone. Cross-hatching adds a second set of lines across the first for deeper tone. Stippling shades with dots; dots closer together look darker. Blending smooths pencil tone with a stump, tissue or finger so no lines show. Scribbling shades with loose, overlapping loops for rough texture. Pressure also controls tone: pressing harder gives darker marks, pressing lightly gives pale marks. Keep the light source in mind — shading must stay darker on the side away from the light. Roman Urdu: hatching lakeeron se, stippling nuqton se shading hai; dabao zyada ho to rang gehra hota hai. Recall first: cover this note and name four shading techniques and what makes each one darker.
Drawing/PE.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Drawing Fundamentals Curriculum
Drawing/PE.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — DM: Drawing section (20)

General Science.body: Vitamins are needed in small amounts, but a shortage causes a named disease. Vitamin A (carrots, milk) — shortage causes night blindness. Vitamin B1 (whole grains) — shortage causes beriberi. Vitamin C (citrus fruits, amla) — shortage causes scurvy, bleeding gums. Vitamin D (sunlight, fish, eggs) — shortage causes rickets in children, weak bones. Vitamin K helps blood clotting. Exam trick: match the vitamin to its disease, not to its food — the paper usually asks the disease. Roman Urdu: vitamin ki kami se kaunsi bimari hoti hai — yehi sawal aata hai. Recall first: cover this note and match A, B1, C and D to night blindness, beriberi, scurvy and rickets.
General Science.title: Vitamins and Deficiency Diseases

General Science.body: Protein builds and repairs the body, especially in growing children. Two protein-deficiency diseases are asked again and again. Kwashiorkor: the child has a swollen belly, thin limbs and stunted growth — it happens when the diet has enough energy but too little protein. Marasmus: the child is very thin and wasted all over — it happens when the diet lacks both protein and energy. Remember: kwashiorkor = swollen belly; marasmus = total wasting. Both are prevented by a balanced diet with milk, eggs, pulses and meat. Recall first: cover this note and explain the difference between kwashiorkor and marasmus in one line each.
General Science.title: Protein-Deficiency Diseases — Kwashiorkor and Marasmus

General Science.body: The human body has three types of muscle. Skeletal muscle is attached to bones and moves the body — it works when we choose (voluntary). Smooth muscle is in the walls of the stomach, intestines and blood vessels — it works on its own (involuntary). Cardiac muscle is only in the heart — it beats without stopping and never tires. Bones give the body shape and protect organs; the skull protects the brain and the ribs protect the heart and lungs. An adult has 206 bones. Recall first: cover this note and name the three muscle types and where each is found.
General Science.title: Muscles and Bones — Three Muscle Types

General Science.body: Photosynthesis is how green plants make food. The plant takes carbon dioxide from the air, water from the soil, and sunlight — the green pigment chlorophyll in the leaves captures the light energy. The products are glucose (food, stored as starch) and oxygen, which is released into the air. The word equation is: carbon dioxide + water → (sunlight, chlorophyll) → glucose + oxygen. Without plants there would be no oxygen for animals to breathe and no food chain. Recall first: cover this note and write the photosynthesis word equation from memory.
General Science.title: Photosynthesis — How Plants Make Food

General Science.body: A flowering plant has roots, stem, leaves and flowers. Roots absorb water and minerals from the soil and hold the plant firm. The stem supports the plant and carries water up and food down. Leaves make food by photosynthesis and lose water through tiny pores called stomata. Flowers are the reproductive part — they make seeds, and seeds grow into new plants. A seed needs water, air and warmth to germinate. Exam tip: root = absorption, stem = transport, leaf = food-making, flower = reproduction. Recall first: cover this note and give the one main job of the root, stem, leaf and flower.
General Science.title: Parts of a Plant and Their Jobs

General Science.body: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. It has three states: solid (fixed shape and volume, e.g. ice), liquid (fixed volume, takes the shape of its container, e.g. water) and gas (no fixed shape or volume, spreads out, e.g. steam). Heating usually changes solid → liquid → gas; cooling reverses it. Gases in the air: nitrogen is about 78%, oxygen about 21%, and carbon dioxide about 0.04%. Air is a mixture, not a compound. Recall first: cover this note and name the three states of matter and the two main gases in air with their percentages.
General Science.title: Matter — Solids, Liquids, Gases and Air

General Science.body: There are eight planets in our solar system, in order from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Mercury is the smallest and closest to the Sun. Venus is the hottest planet and the brightest in the sky. Earth is the only known planet with life. Mars is called the Red Planet. Jupiter is the largest planet. Saturn is famous for its rings. Neptune is the farthest from the Sun. The Sun is a star, not a planet, and the Moon is Earth's satellite. Recall first: cover this note and list the eight planets in order from the Sun.
General Science.title: The Solar System — Eight Planets in Order

General Science.body: Energy is the ability to do work. Renewable energy comes from sources that do not run out: sunlight (solar), wind, flowing water (hydropower) and geothermal heat. Non-renewable energy comes from fuels that run out: coal, oil and natural gas (fossil fuels). Burning fossil fuels gives energy but pollutes the air; renewable sources are cleaner but depend on weather and place. Forms of energy include heat, light, sound, electrical and kinetic (movement) energy. A fan changes electrical energy into kinetic energy. Recall first: cover this note and sort solar, wind, coal, oil, hydropower and natural gas into renewable and non-renewable.
General Science.title: Energy — Renewable and Non-Renewable Sources

Arabic.body: Nahw (نحو) is Arabic syntax — it studies how words join into sentences and what case ending (i'rab) each word takes. Sarf (صرف) is morphology — it studies how words themselves are built, e.g. how one root gives many words. Simple way to remember: Nahw = sentence rules, Sarf = word-building rules. Roman Urdu: Nahw jumlay ke qawaneen, Sarf lafzon ki banawat. In the AT paper both are tested, so learn the difference first. Recall first: cover this note and say in your own words what Nahw and Sarf each study.
Arabic.title: Nahw vs Sarf — Syntax and Morphology

Arabic.body: Every Arabic word is one of three types. Ism (اسم) is a noun — a person, place or thing, e.g. كِتَاب (book), عَلِيّ (Ali). Fi'l (فعل) is a verb — an action linked to time, e.g. كَتَبَ (he wrote), يَكْتُبُ (he writes). Harf (حرف) is a particle — it has no complete meaning alone, e.g. فِي (in), مِنْ (from), إِلَى (to). Test trick: if a word takes tanween or al-, it is an Ism; if it shows past/present time, it is a Fi'l. Recall first: cover this note and name the three word types with one example of each.
Arabic.title: Three Word Types — Ism, Fi'l, Harf

Arabic.body: I'rab (إعراب) is the case ending on a word — the short vowel at its end that shows its job in the sentence. Marfu' (مرفوع) is the nominative case, usually damma (ـُ), e.g. the subject (Fa'il) is Marfu'. Mansub (منصوب) is the accusative case, usually fatha (ـَ), e.g. the object (Maf'ul) is Mansub. Majrur (مجرور) is the genitive case, usually kasra (ـِ), e.g. a word after a preposition (Harf al-Jarr) is Majrur. Roman Urdu: damma = Marfu', fatha = Mansub, kasra = Majrur. Recall first: cover this note and match damma, fatha and kasra to Marfu', Mansub and Majrur.
Arabic.title: I'rab — Marfu', Mansub, Majrur

Arabic.body: A nominal sentence (الجملة الاسمية) starts with a noun. It has two parts: Mubtada' (مبتدأ) — the subject, what we talk about — and Khabar (خبر) — the news about it. Example: اَلْكِتَابُ جَدِيدٌ (The book is new) — al-Kitabu is the Mubtada', jadeedun is the Khabar. Both are usually Marfu' (damma). Roman Urdu: pehle ism aaye to jumla Ismiyyah hota hai; pehla hissa Mubtada', doosra Khabar. Recall first: cover this note and build one nominal sentence of your own, naming its Mubtada' and Khabar.
Arabic.title: Nominal Sentence — Mubtada' and Khabar

Arabic.body: A verbal sentence (الجملة الفعلية) starts with a verb. Its parts are: Fi'l (فعل) — the verb; Fa'il (فاعل) — the doer, always Marfu'; and Maf'ul bihi (مفعول به) — the object, always Mansub. Arabic word order is usually verb first: كَتَبَ عَلِيٌّ اَلدَّرْسَ (Ali wrote the lesson) — kataba = Fi'l, Aliyyun = Fa'il, ad-darsa = Maf'ul. This VSO order (verb-subject-object) is the opposite of English and Urdu, so practise it until it feels natural. Recall first: cover this note and break كَتَبَ عَلِيٌّ اَلدَّرْسَ into Fi'l, Fa'il and Maf'ul.
Arabic.title: Verbal Sentence — Fi'l, Fa'il, Maf'ul

Arabic.body: Most Arabic words grow from a three-letter root (جذر). Example: the root ك-ت-ب (k-t-b) is about writing — كِتَاب (kitab, book), كَاتِب (katib, writer), مَكْتُوب (maktub, written), مَكْتَبَة (maktaba, library). Learn the root and you can guess new words: same letters, related meaning. Sarf studies these patterns (awzan). Test tip: when a question asks for the root of a word, strip the extra letters and keep the three core letters. Recall first: cover this note and list three words from the root ك-ت-ب with their meanings.
Arabic.title: Three-Letter Roots — One Root, Many Words

Arabic.body: Demonstratives (أسماء الإشارة) point to things. Near: هَذَا (hadha, this — masculine), هَذِهِ (hadhihi, this — feminine), هَؤُلَاءِ (ha'ula'i, these). Far: ذَلِكَ (dhalika, that — masculine), تِلْكَ (tilka, that — feminine), أُولَئِكَ (ula'ika, those). Example: هَذَا كِتَابٌ (This is a book), تِلْكَ مَدْرَسَةٌ (That is a school). Common exam trap: matching the wrong gender — hadha goes with masculine nouns, hadhihi with feminine. Recall first: cover this note and write the Arabic for 'this book' (masculine) and 'that school' (feminine).
Arabic.title: Demonstratives — Hadha, Hadhihi, Dhalika, Tilka

Arabic.body: Arabic nouns have three numbers: singular (مفرد), dual (مثنى, exactly two — formed by adding انِ or ينِ, e.g. كِتَابَانِ = two books) and plural (جمع, three or more). Gender is masculine (مذكر) or feminine (مؤنث) — feminine nouns often end in ة (ta marbuta), e.g. مَدْرَسَة (school). Sound plurals add ونَ/ينَ (masculine) or اتٌ (feminine); broken plurals change the word shape, e.g. كِتَاب → كُتُب. Exam tip: dual is the number most students forget — remember it means exactly two. Recall first: cover this note and give the dual of كِتَاب and the plural of كِتَاب.
Arabic.title: Gender and Number — Singular, Dual, Plural
Al-Fa'il — The Doer (الفاعل) in Nahw (النحو)
Arabic.body: Al-Fa'il (الفاعل) is the noun that does the action of the verb — the doer or subject of a verbal sentence — in the science of Nahw (النحو), which studies sentence structure and case endings. It is always Marfu' (in the nominative, Raf' state). It normally comes after the verb: verb, then doer, then object. Its usual sign of Raf' is Damma — for a singular noun, a broken plural and a sound feminine plural. Waw is the sign of Raf' for a sound masculine plural and for the five special nouns (father, brother, father-in-law, mouth, possessor of). Alif is the sign of Raf' for a dual noun (two of something). The Fa'il can be a plain noun or a hidden or attached pronoun. Example: كَتَبَ عَلِيٌّ اَلدَّرْسَ (Ali wrote the lesson) — kataba is the Fi'l, Aliyyun is the Fa'il, ad-darsa is the Maf'ul. Recall first: cover this note and give the Raf' sign of the Fa'il for a dual noun and for a sound masculine plural.
Arabic.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Al-Muqaddimah al-Ajurrumiyyah

Arabic.title: Al-Maf'ul Bihi — The Object (المفعول به)
Arabic.body: Al-Maf'ul Bihi (المفعول به) is the noun or pronoun that the verb's action falls upon — who or what is affected by the action. It is always Mansub (in the accusative, Nasb state). Its usual sign of Nasb is Fatha — for a singular noun and a broken plural. Ya is the sign of Nasb for a dual noun and for a sound masculine plural. Kasra is the sign of Nasb for a sound feminine plural — an exception to the usual Fatha. Alif is the sign of Nasb for the five special nouns. It can also be an attached pronoun on the verb, or a separate pronoun form. Example: كَتَبَ عَلِيٌّ اَلدَّرْسَ (Ali wrote the lesson) — ad-darsa is the Maf'ul Bihi, Mansub with Fatha. Recall first: cover this note and say which sign marks Nasb for a sound feminine plural object, and why it is an exception.

Arabic.title: Al-Mubtada' and Al-Khabar in Detail (المبتدأ والخبر)
Arabic.body: Al-Mubtada' (المبتدأ) and Al-Khabar (الخبر) together make a nominal sentence (Jumla Ismiyya), a sentence that starts with a noun and needs no verb. Al-Mubtada' is the topic — what the sentence is about. Al-Khabar is what is said about it — the information that completes the meaning. Both are always Marfu'. The Khabar must agree with the Mubtada' in number and gender. Usually the Mubtada' is definite and the Khabar is indefinite. A Khabar need not be a single word: it can be a single noun or adjective, a prepositional phrase, a word of place, a verb with its own doer, or a whole sentence of its own. The order can also be reversed, with the Khabar first and the Mubtada' after. Example: اَلْكِتَابُ كَبِيرٌ (the book is big) — al-kitabu is the Mubtada', kabirun is the Khabar. Recall first: cover this note and break اَلْكِتَابُ كَبِيرٌ into Mubtada' and Khabar.

Arabic.title: Sarf — Roots and Verb Patterns (صرف)
Arabic.body: Sarf is the study of word shapes: how one root grows into many related words. Nahw, by contrast, studies how words work in a sentence. Most Arabic words come from a three-letter root, and the pattern (Wazn) is shown with the model letters ف ع ل. Take the root ك ت ب (writing): kataba means he wrote, yaktubu means he writes, uktub means write (command), katib means writer, kitab means book, maktub means written, and maktab means office or desk — all from the same three letters. Past tense (Madi) is built by adding suffixes to the root; the base 'he' form has no suffix. Present tense (Mudari') is built with a prefix (one of ا ت ي ن) and sometimes a suffix, and it also covers future meaning. The command (Amr) is built from the present tense, dropping the prefix and adding an opening Alif where needed for pronunciation. Recall first: cover this note and derive katib, kitab and maktab from the root ك ت ب.

Arabic.title: I'rab Signs — How Case Endings Show (إعراب)
Arabic.body: I'rab is the change in a word's ending that shows its job in the sentence. Raf' (nominative) is usually shown by Damma, by Waw for a sound masculine plural and the five special nouns, and by Alif for a dual noun. Nasb (accusative) is usually shown by Fatha, by Ya for a dual noun and a sound masculine plural, by Kasra for a sound feminine plural, and by Alif for the five special nouns. Jarr (genitive) is usually shown by Kasra, by Ya for a dual noun and a sound masculine plural, and by Fatha for words that do not take Tanween. The Fa'il is always Marfu', the Maf'ul Bihi is always Mansub, and a noun after a preposition is always Majrur. Learn the signs by word type, not by memorising the table alone: singular, dual, sound masculine plural, sound feminine plural, broken plural and the five nouns each have their own pattern. Recall first: cover this note and give the Raf' and Nasb signs for a dual noun.
Arabic.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Al-Muqaddimah al-Ajurrumiyyah

Pedagogy.body: Bloom's Taxonomy lists six levels of thinking: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyse, Evaluate and Create (revised version, Anderson & Krathwohl). Lower levels ask for recall and explanation; higher levels ask for analysis, judgement and making something new. A question like 'Define photosynthesis' tests Remember; 'Design an experiment' tests Create. Teachers should move students from lower to higher levels. Exam tip: the revised order is Remember → Understand → Apply → Analyse → Evaluate → Create.
Pedagogy.title: Bloom's Taxonomy — Levels of Learning

Pedagogy.body: Jean Piaget described four stages: Sensorimotor (birth–2 years, learning through senses and movement), Preoperational (2–7 years, symbolic play but egocentric thinking), Concrete Operational (7–11 years, logical thinking about real objects) and Formal Operational (11+ years, abstract and hypothetical thinking). A child in the concrete stage can conserve number and volume but struggles with abstract ideas. Teachers should match tasks to the child's stage and use concrete material before abstract concepts.
Pedagogy.title: Piaget's Stages of Cognitive Development

Pedagogy.body: Erik Erikson proposed eight stages of psychosocial development across life, each with a crisis to resolve. For school children the key stages are Initiative vs Guilt (3–6 years), Industry vs Inferiority (6–12 years) and Identity vs Role Confusion (adolescence). If a child of 8 is encouraged and praised for effort, they develop industry (competence); repeated failure breeds inferiority. Teachers build confidence by giving achievable tasks and recognising effort, not only results.
Pedagogy.title: Erikson's Psychosocial Stages

Pedagogy.body: A good lesson plan has clear objectives (what students will learn), a starter, the main teaching activity, guided and independent practice, and a closing/assessment. Objectives should be SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Start with what students already know (previous knowledge) and link the new lesson to it. Always plan for different abilities — give extra support to weak students and extension work to fast learners. A plan without an objective is just a list of activities.
Pedagogy.title: Lesson Planning — The Essentials

Pedagogy.body: Formative assessment happens DURING learning to guide teaching — quizzes, classwork, observation, homework feedback. Summative assessment happens AFTER learning to judge achievement — final exams, board exams, end-of-term tests. Formative is assessment FOR learning; summative is assessment OF learning. Diagnostic assessment finds what students already know before teaching starts. Good teachers use formative checks daily so that the summative result holds no surprises.
Pedagogy.title: Formative vs Summative Assessment

Pedagogy.body: Lev Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) is the gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with help. Scaffolding is the temporary support a teacher gives inside the ZPD — hints, worked examples, breaking a task into steps — and it is removed gradually as the learner becomes independent. Examples: modelling a solved problem first, giving sentence starters, or peer support. Scaffolding is not doing the work for the student; it is support that fades.
Pedagogy.title: Scaffolding and the Zone of Proximal Development

Pedagogy.body: Collaborative learning means students learn together in pairs or groups — think-pair-share, group projects and peer tutoring. It builds communication, teamwork and deeper understanding, but the teacher must give clear roles so one student does not do all the work. Learning styles describe preferences: visual learners learn from pictures and diagrams, auditory learners from listening, and kinaesthetic learners from doing and moving. Good teaching uses a mix of all three rather than labelling a child as only one type.
Pedagogy.title: Collaborative Learning and Learning Styles

Pedagogy.body: Vygotsky said children learn first through social interaction and then inside their own minds — learning is social before it is individual. Two of his ideas matter most here. The More Knowledgeable Other (MKO) is anyone who knows more — a teacher, a parent or a brighter classmate — and helps the learner. Language drives thought: children first talk aloud to guide themselves (private speech) and later think in silent inner speech. A classroom built on Vygotsky uses discussion, group work and guided help. Note: his Zone of Proximal Development and scaffolding are covered in a separate note in this library — read that one with this. Recall first: cover this note and explain what the More Knowledgeable Other is and how language drives thought.
Pedagogy.title: Vygotsky — Social Learning and the More Knowledgeable Other

Pedagogy.body: Lawrence Kohlberg described moral development in three levels with six stages. Level 1 — Pre-conventional (young children): stage 1 obey to avoid punishment, stage 2 act for reward or self-interest. Level 2 — Conventional (most adolescents and adults): stage 3 act to be seen as good by others, stage 4 follow laws and rules to keep order. Level 3 — Post-conventional (few adults): stage 5 follow social contracts and rights, stage 6 follow universal ethical principles. He tested this with the Heinz dilemma — should a man steal a drug to save his dying wife? Exam tip: learn the three levels first, then the two stages inside each. Recall first: cover this note and name Kohlberg's three levels and what each is based on.
Pedagogy.title: Kohlberg — Levels of Moral Development

Pedagogy.body: Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs is a pyramid of five levels, from bottom to top: (1) physiological needs — food, water, sleep; (2) safety needs — security, shelter; (3) love and belonging — family, friends; (4) esteem — respect, confidence; (5) self-actualisation — reaching one's full potential. Lower needs must be mostly met before higher needs motivate a person. For teachers the lesson is practical: a hungry, tired or frightened child cannot concentrate on learning, so basic needs come first. Exam tip: the order from bottom to top is the question — learn it as a ladder. Recall first: cover this note and list Maslow's five levels from bottom to top.
Pedagogy.title: Maslow — Hierarchy of Needs

Pedagogy.body: B. F. Skinner studied operant conditioning — learning from the consequences of behaviour. Positive reinforcement adds something pleasant (praise, a star) to increase a behaviour. Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant (no homework tonight) to increase a behaviour — it is still reinforcement, not punishment. Punishment decreases a behaviour: positive punishment adds something unpleasant, negative punishment removes something pleasant. Extinction is when a behaviour fades because it is no longer reinforced. A teacher uses reinforcement far more than punishment because it builds the behaviour wanted. Recall first: cover this note and explain the difference between negative reinforcement and punishment.
Pedagogy.title: Skinner — Operant Conditioning and Reinforcement

Pedagogy.body: Jerome Bruner said learning should follow a spiral curriculum — the same topic is revisited again and again, each time at a deeper and more complex level. A child first meets fractions with real objects, later with pictures, later with symbols. He also named three modes of representation: enactive (learning by doing and handling objects), iconic (learning through images and diagrams) and symbolic (learning through words and symbols). He supported discovery learning — students finding answers by exploring, with the teacher guiding rather than telling. Roman Urdu: aik hi mauzu baar baar, har dafa gehra — yehi spiral curriculum hai. Recall first: cover this note and explain the spiral curriculum and the three modes enactive, iconic and symbolic.
Pedagogy.title: Bruner — Spiral Curriculum and Modes of Representation

Pedagogy.body: A portfolio is a purposeful collection of a student's work over time — essays, drawings, projects and tests — that shows progress, not just one result. A rubric is a scoring guide: it lists the criteria for good work (e.g. content, organisation, language) and describes each level of quality, so marking is fair and clear to the student. Percentile rank is a test score meaning: a percentile rank of 70 means the student scored better than 70% of the group. Portfolios and rubrics belong mainly to formative assessment — they guide learning while it happens — while final exams are summative. (The formative vs summative difference itself is covered in a separate note in this library.) Recall first: cover this note and explain what a portfolio shows, what a rubric lists, and what a percentile rank of 70 means.
Pedagogy.title: Portfolios, Rubrics and Percentile Rank

Pak Studies.body: The Two-Nation Theory held that Hindus and Muslims were two separate nations. The All-India Muslim League was founded in Dhaka in 1906. The Lahore Resolution was passed on 23 March 1940, demanding separate states for Muslims. The 1945-46 elections gave the Muslim League a sweeping victory in Muslim seats. Pakistan came into being on 14 August 1947 under the leadership of Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah. 23 March is celebrated as Pakistan Day; 14 August as Independence Day.
Pak Studies.title: Pakistan Movement — Key Milestones

Pak Studies.body: Muhammad Ali Jinnah was born on 25 December 1876 in Karachi. He joined the Muslim League in 1913 and became its permanent leader. His Fourteen Points (1929) defended Muslim rights after the Nehru Report. He was the first Governor-General of Pakistan and served from 14 August 1947 until his death on 11 September 1948. His motto was 'Unity, Faith and Discipline'. His mausoleum (Mazar-e-Quaid) is in Karachi.
Pak Studies.title: Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah

Pak Studies.body: The 1973 Constitution was passed on 10 April 1973 and came into force on 14 August 1973. It declares Pakistan an Islamic Republic and Islam the state religion. It provides a parliamentary system, a bicameral legislature (National Assembly and Senate) and fundamental rights for citizens. It has been amended many times; the 18th Amendment (2010) gave provinces greater autonomy. It is the longest-serving constitution of Pakistan.
Pak Studies.title: 1973 Constitution of Pakistan

Pak Studies.body: Liaquat Ali Khan was the first Prime Minister of Pakistan (1947–1951). Khawaja Nazimuddin was the second Prime Minister and later became Governor-General. Benazir Bhutto was the first woman Prime Minister of Pakistan and of the Muslim world. Zulfikar Ali Bhutto was the first civilian Martial Law Administrator and later Prime Minister. Iskander Mirza was the first President of Pakistan (1956). General Ayub Khan was the first military ruler.
Pak Studies.title: Prime Ministers and Presidents — Firsts

Pak Studies.body: Pakistan covers about 796,096 square kilometres and shares borders with India, China, Afghanistan and Iran, with the Arabian Sea to the south. The Indus River is the longest river; the K2 (8,611 m) in Gilgit-Baltistan is the second-highest mountain in the world. Punjab is the most populous province; Balochistan is the largest by area. The capital is Islamabad; the largest city is Karachi. The main passes are Khyber Pass and Bolan Pass.
Pak Studies.title: Geography of Pakistan

Pak Studies.body: The first Constituent Assembly adopted the Objectives Resolution in March 1949. The first Martial Law was imposed in 1958 by General Ayub Khan. East Pakistan separated in December 1971 and became Bangladesh. The 1973 Constitution restored parliamentary democracy. General Zia-ul-Haq imposed Martial Law in 1977. Pakistan became a declared nuclear power after tests on 28 May 1998 (Youm-e-Takbeer). The 18th Amendment was passed in 2010.
Pak Studies.title: Major Events After Independence

Pak Studies.body: Pakistan has four provinces (Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan), plus Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Jammu and Kashmir. Major rivers are the Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej. Tarbela Dam on the Indus is one of the largest earth-filled dams in the world; Mangla Dam is on the Jhelum. The Thar Desert is in Sindh; the Thal Desert is in Punjab. Lahore is called the cultural capital; Peshawar is one of the oldest cities of South Asia.
Pak Studies.title: Provinces, Rivers and Dams

Islamiyat.body: The Holy Quran has 114 Surahs and 30 Parahs (Juz). Surahs revealed in Makkah before Hijrat are called Makki; those revealed in Madinah after Hijrat are Madani. Makki Surahs are usually shorter and focus on Tawhid, the Hereafter and moral character. Madani Surahs are longer and contain laws about worship, society, economy and jihad. Surah Al-Fatiha is the first Surah; Surah Al-Baqarah is the longest; Surah Al-Kausar is the shortest.
Islamiyat.title: Quran: Surahs, Parahs and Revelation

Islamiyat.body: Makki Surahs often begin with 'Ya Ayyuhan Naas' (O mankind) and discuss belief, the Day of Judgement and the stories of past prophets. Madani Surahs often begin with 'Ya Ayyuhal Lazina Aamanu' (O you who believe) and give practical laws. The first revealed verses were the first five verses of Surah Al-Alaq, revealed in Cave Hira in 610 AD. The last revealed verse is generally held to be verse 281 of Surah Al-Baqarah. Remember: revelation continued for about 23 years.
Islamiyat.title: Makki and Madani Surahs — How to Tell Them Apart

Islamiyat.body: Sihah Sitta means the six authentic books of Hadith: Sahih Bukhari (Imam Muhammad ibn Ismail Bukhari), Sahih Muslim (Imam Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj), Sunan Abu Dawood (Imam Abu Dawood), Jami Tirmidhi (Imam Muhammad ibn Isa Tirmidhi), Sunan Nasai (Imam Ahmad ibn Shuayb Nasai) and Sunan Ibn Majah (Imam Muhammad ibn Yazid Ibn Majah). Sahih Bukhari and Sahih Muslim are the most authentic and are called Sahihain (the two Sahihs). Imam Bukhari was born in 194 AH in Bukhara. For MCQs, remember the book-author pairs, not Hadith numbers.
Islamiyat.title: Sihah Sitta — The Six Authentic Hadith Books

Islamiyat.body: The Prophet Muhammad (SAW) was born in Makkah in 571 AD, the Year of the Elephant (Aam al-Feel). He received the first revelation at age 40 in 610 AD in Cave Hira. He migrated to Madinah (Hijrat) in 622 AD, which marks the start of the Islamic calendar. The Battle of Badr was fought in 2 AH, Uhud in 3 AH, Khandaq (Trench) in 5 AH and the Conquest of Makkah (Fatah Makkah) in 8 AH. The Prophet (SAW) passed away in 11 AH in Madinah.
Islamiyat.title: Seerat: Key Dates of the Prophet's Life (SAW)

Islamiyat.body: Badr (2 AH): 313 Muslims against about 1000 Quraish; a great victory. Uhud (3 AH): Muslims suffered losses after archers left their post on the hill. Khandaq (5 AH): a trench was dug around Madinah on the advice of Salman Farsi (RA); the enemy siege failed. Khyber (7 AH): the Jewish forts were conquered. Fatah Makkah (8 AH): Makkah was conquered almost without bloodshed and a general amnesty was announced. Hunain (8 AH) followed Fatah Makkah; Tabuk (9 AH) was the last major expedition.
Islamiyat.title: Ghazwat — The Major Battles

Islamiyat.body: The order is: Hazrat Abu Bakr Siddique (RA) 11–13 AH, Hazrat Umar Farooq (RA) 13–23 AH, Hazrat Usman Ghani (RA) 23–35 AH and Hazrat Ali (RA) 35–40 AH. Abu Bakr (RA) compiled the Quran and fought the wars against false prophets. Umar (RA) expanded the Islamic state greatly and set up the Diwan (register) and the Hijri calendar. Usman (RA) standardised the written Quran. Ali (RA) was the first child to accept Islam and the fourth Caliph.
Islamiyat.title: Khulafa-e-Rashideen — The Four Rightly Guided Caliphs

Islamiyat.body: The five pillars are: Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salah (prayer five times a day), Zakat (obligatory charity, 2.5% on qualifying wealth held for a lunar year), Saum (fasting in Ramadan) and Hajj (pilgrimage to Makkah once in a lifetime for those who can afford it). Salah was made obligatory on the night of Miraj. Zakat is due on gold, silver, cash, trade goods and livestock above the Nisab. Fasting was made obligatory in 2 AH.
Islamiyat.title: Arkan-e-Islam — The Five Pillars

Islamiyat.body: Hajj is performed in the month of Zil Hajj; its main rites run from 8 to 13 Zil Hajj. The Wuquf (standing) at Arafat on 9 Zil Hajj is the most important rite — Hajj is incomplete without it. Tawaf is circling the Kaaba seven times; Sa'i is walking between Safa and Marwa seven times. Pilgrims stay at Mina, go to Arafat, then Muzdalifah, and throw pebbles (Rami) at the Jamarat. Ihram is the special state and dress for Hajj and Umrah; Umrah can be performed at any time of the year.
Islamiyat.title: Hajj — Key Facts

Islamiyat.body: The main sources of Islamic law are the Quran, Sunnah, Ijma (consensus of scholars) and Qiyas (analogy). The four Sunni schools of Fiqh are Hanafi (Imam Abu Hanifa), Maliki (Imam Malik), Shafi'i (Imam Shafi'i) and Hanbali (Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal). Hanafi is the most followed school in Pakistan. Fiqh divides actions into Fard (obligatory), Wajib (necessary), Sunnah, Mustahab (recommended), Mubah (allowed), Makruh (disliked) and Haram (forbidden). Wudu has four Fard acts: washing the face, washing both arms up to the elbows, wiping a part of the head (Masah), and washing both feet up to the ankles.
Islamiyat.title: Fiqh Basics — Sources and Schools

Islamiyat.body: Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA) is called Siddique (the Truthful); Hazrat Umar (RA) is Farooq (the one who distinguishes truth from falsehood); Hazrat Usman (RA) is Zun-Nurain (possessor of two lights); Hazrat Ali (RA) is Asadullah (Lion of Allah). Hazrat Khadija (RA) was the first wife of the Prophet (SAW) and the first person to accept Islam. Hazrat Bilal (RA) was the first Muazzin. Hazrat Zaid ibn Harithah (RA) is the only companion mentioned by name in the Quran. Hazrat Ayesha (RA) narrated many Hadith.
Islamiyat.title: Important Islamic Personalities and Titles
Wahi — The First Revelation (وحی)
Islamiyat.body: Wahi is revelation: Allah's message sent to a Prophet. The first revelation came to Prophet Muhammad (SAW) in Cave Hira, near Makkah, in the month of Ramadan, around 610 CE, when he was 40 years old. The first revealed words were the opening five verses of Surah Al-Alaq, beginning with the command to read and recite. Revelation continued for about 23 years — about 13 years in Makkah and about 10 years in Madinah — and it came down in portions, as events and questions needed guidance. Makki revelation stresses faith, the afterlife and the stories of past prophets; Madani revelation covers law, family and community life. Recall first: cover this note and say where, when and with which Surah the first revelation began.
Islamiyat.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Riwaq Al Quran

Islamiyat.title: Hadith — What It Is and How It Is Preserved (حدیث)
Islamiyat.body: Hadith is the record of the Prophet's words, actions and approvals — the Sunnah, the Prophet's example, which explains and applies the Quran. Each Hadith has two parts: the Isnad, the chain of narrators who passed it on, and the Matn, the text itself. Scholars judged a narration by its chain and its text, and collected the sound ones into books. The six canonical Sunni collections are called Sihah Sitta (the Six Books): Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, Sunan Abi Dawud, Jami' at-Tirmidhi, Sunan an-Nasa'i and Sunan Ibn Majah. Bukhari and Muslim together are called the Sahihayn (the Two Sahihs); both aimed to include only authenticated narrations, and Bukhari is ranked first by most Sunni scholars. The other four are arranged more by legal topic. Exact Hadith totals per book vary by edition and by whether repetitions are counted, so they are not given as settled numbers here. Recall first: cover this note and name the six books and the two called the Sahihayn.
Islamiyat.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Wikipedia (Kutub al-Sittah)

Islamiyat.title: Seerat — The Hijrah and the Madani Period (ہجرت)
Islamiyat.body: The Hijrah is the migration of the Prophet (SAW) and the Muslims from Makkah to Madinah in 622 CE — Year 1 of the Hijri calendar. In Madinah the Masjid al-Nabawi was built, the Charter of Madinah was agreed, and a Muslim community took shape. The first major battle was Badr, in 624 CE (2 AH): about 313 Muslims faced a Quraysh force of about 1,000. Uhud followed in 625 CE (3 AH), a near-victory that turned to heavy loss when archers left their post. The Battle of Khandaq (the Trench) came in 627 CE (5 AH), when Madinah was defended by a trench and the besieging coalition withdrew. The Treaty of Hudaybiyya was agreed in 628 CE (6 AH), Makkah was conquered in 630 CE (8 AH), and the Farewell Pilgrimage and the Prophet's passing came in 632 CE. Recall first: cover this note and put Badr, Uhud and Khandaq in order with their years.

Islamiyat.title: Fiqh — The Four Schools and Their Founders (فقہ)
Islamiyat.body: Fiqh means deep understanding: the scholarly derivation of practical rulings for worship, transactions, family and society. Its four commonly listed Sunni sources are the Quran, the Sunnah, Ijma (consensus of qualified scholars) and Qiyas (analogical reasoning from a known case to a new case sharing the same effective cause). Imam al-Shafi'i systematised this four-source list in his work Al-Risala. The four Sunni schools are the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools — all accept the same four sources but differ in method and emphasis. Hanafi: Imam Abu Hanifa (Kufa, Iraq), noted for reasoned opinion and analogy. Maliki: Imam Malik ibn Anas (Madinah), who gives great weight to the practice of the people of Madinah and compiled Al-Muwatta. Shafi'i: Imam Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i, founder of legal theory as a formal discipline. Hanbali: Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal (Baghdad), a Hadith scholar, the most text-based of the four in approach. Recall first: cover this note and match each school to its founder and city.

Maths.body: A fraction has a numerator (top) and a denominator (bottom). To add or subtract fractions, first make the denominators equal using the LCM. To multiply, multiply numerators together and denominators together. To divide, multiply by the reciprocal of the second fraction (flip it). To compare fractions, convert them to the same denominator or to decimals. Simplify by dividing both parts by their HCF. Example: 3/4 + 1/4 = 1.
Maths.title: Fractions — Basics and Operations

Maths.body: HCF (Highest Common Factor) is the largest number that divides two or more numbers exactly; find it by listing factors or by prime factorisation. LCM (Lowest Common Multiple) is the smallest number that is a multiple of two or more numbers. For two numbers, LCM × HCF = product of the numbers. Example: HCF of 12 and 18 is 6; LCM of 12 and 18 is 36. LCM is used for fraction addition and for problems about bells ringing together or buses leaving together.
Maths.title: LCM and HCF

Maths.body: Percent means 'out of 100'. To find x% of a number, multiply the number by x and divide by 100. Percentage increase = (increase ÷ original) × 100. Profit % = (profit ÷ cost price) × 100; loss % = (loss ÷ cost price) × 100. To increase a number by 20%, multiply by 1.20; to decrease by 20%, multiply by 0.80. Common conversions: 50% = 1/2, 25% = 1/4, 20% = 1/5, 10% = 1/10, 12.5% = 1/8.
Maths.title: Percentages — The Exam Favourite

Maths.body: A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind, written a:b. To divide a quantity in a ratio, add the parts, then give each share its part of the total. If A:B = 2:3 and the total is 50, A gets 2/5 × 50 = 20 and B gets 30. In direct proportion, as one quantity increases the other increases; in inverse proportion, one increases while the other decreases. Unitary method: find the value of one unit first, then multiply. Always check that units match before forming a ratio.
Maths.title: Ratio and Proportion

Maths.body: An equation has two sides joined by '='; whatever you do to one side, do to the other. To solve x + 7 = 15, subtract 7 from both sides: x = 8. To solve 3x = 21, divide both sides by 3: x = 7. (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2; (a − b)^2 = a^2 − 2ab + b^2; a^2 − b^2 = (a + b)(a − b). Remember BODMAS order: Brackets, Orders (powers), Division/Multiplication, Addition/Subtraction. Check your answer by putting x back into the original equation.
Maths.title: Algebra — Equations and Simplification

Maths.body: Age problems are solved by setting up equations. Let the unknown age be x; '5 years ago' means x − 5, 'after 5 years' means x + 5. Example: Ali is 3 times as old as his son; in 10 years he will be twice as old — set 3x + 10 = 2(x + 10) and solve. For work problems: if A finishes a job in 6 days and B in 12 days, together they do 1/6 + 1/12 = 1/4 of the job per day, so 4 days together. Read the question twice and underline the numbers before calculating.
Maths.title: Age Problems and Word Problems

Maths.body: Average = sum of all values ÷ number of values. To find a missing number, use: sum = average × count. Speed = distance ÷ time; distance = speed × time. Simple Interest = (Principal × Rate × Time) ÷ 100. Example: Rs 10,000 at 5% for 2 years gives interest of Rs 1,000. For averages, remember that adding the same number to every value raises the average by that number. For speed problems, convert minutes to hours before dividing.
Maths.title: Average, Speed and Simple Interest

GK.body: Capitals of Pakistan's neighbours and important countries: Pakistan — Islamabad; India — New Delhi; China — Beijing; Afghanistan — Kabul; Iran — Tehran; Bangladesh — Dhaka; Sri Lanka — Colombo; Nepal — Kathmandu; United Kingdom — London; United States — Washington, D.C.; Saudi Arabia — Riyadh; Turkey — Ankara; Russia — Moscow; Japan — Tokyo; Australia — Canberra. Exam trick: do not confuse Australia's capital (Canberra, not Sydney) or Turkey's (Ankara, not Istanbul). Learn them in pairs with the country, not alone. Recall first: cover this note and write the capitals of Pakistan, India, China, Afghanistan, Iran, the UK and Australia.
GK.title: Capitals of Important Countries

GK.body: The United Nations (UN) was founded in 1945 after the Second World War to keep peace between countries; its headquarters is in New York and it has 193 member states. Its main organs include the General Assembly (all members), the Security Council (15 members, 5 permanent with veto power) and the International Court of Justice (at The Hague). Pakistan joined the UN in 1947. The UN's Secretary-General is its chief officer. Roman Urdu: UN ka maqsad aman qaim rakhna hai; is ke 193 member mulk hain. Recall first: cover this note and say when the UN was founded, where its headquarters is, and how many members it has.
GK.title: The United Nations (UN)

GK.body: Three regional organisations are asked often. OIC (Organisation of Islamic Cooperation): the organisation of Muslim countries, headquarters in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia; it has 57 member states. SAARC (South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation): the organisation of South Asian countries, headquarters in Kathmandu, Nepal; it has 8 members — Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan, Maldives and Afghanistan. ECO (Economic Cooperation Organization): headquarters in Tehran, Iran; it has 10 members including Pakistan, Iran and Turkey. Learn each as name + headquarters + members. Recall first: cover this note and match OIC, SAARC and ECO to Jeddah, Kathmandu and Tehran.
GK.title: OIC, SAARC and ECO — Headquarters and Members

GK.body: The main dams of Pakistan: Tarbela Dam on the Indus River in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa — one of the largest earth-filled dams in the world. Mangla Dam on the Jhelum River in Azad Kashmir. Warsak Dam on the Kabul River near Peshawar. Diamer-Bhasha Dam on the Indus is under construction. A dam stores river water for irrigation, drinking water, flood control and hydroelectric power. Exam tip: always pair the dam with its river — Tarbela-Indus, Mangla-Jhelum, Warsak-Kabul. Recall first: cover this note and match Tarbela, Mangla and Warsak to their rivers.
GK.title: Dams of Pakistan and Their Rivers

GK.body: The rivers of Pakistan: the Indus is the longest river of Pakistan and flows from the north to the Arabian Sea. Its eastern tributaries are the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej — together with the Indus they form the Indus river system. The Kabul River joins the Indus near Attock. The Indus is the lifeline of Pakistan's agriculture, feeding the world's largest canal irrigation system. Memory aid: Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej — learn them in that west-to-east order. Recall first: cover this note and list the five eastern tributaries of the Indus in order.
GK.title: Rivers of Pakistan — The Indus System

GK.body: National facts of Pakistan: the national language is Urdu; the national anthem was written by Hafeez Jalandhari; the national animal is the Markhor; the national bird is the Chukar partridge; the national flower is Jasmine; the national tree is the Deodar; the national sport is field hockey; the national fruit is the mango; the national drink is sugarcane juice (commonly cited). The flag is dark green with a white stripe, a white crescent and star. Pakistan's independence day is 14 August 1947. Recall first: cover this note and name the national animal, bird, flower, sport and language of Pakistan.
GK.title: National Symbols and Facts of Pakistan

Urdu.body: اسم وہ لفظ ہے جو کسی شخص، جگہ یا چیز کا نام ہو، جیسے علی، لاہور، کتاب۔ فعل وہ لفظ ہے جس سے کام کا ہونا ظاہر ہو، جیسے کھانا، جانا، پڑھنا۔ صفت وہ لفظ ہے جو اسم کی خوبی یا خامی بتائے، جیسے اچھا، بڑا، خوبصورت۔ ضمیر وہ لفظ ہے جو اسم کی جگہ آئے، جیسے وہ، میں، تم۔ امتحان میں اکثر اسم کی اقسام (اسم معرفہ، اسم نکرہ) اور فعل کی اقسام (فعل ماضی، فعل حال، فعل مستقبل) پوچھے جاتے ہیں۔
Urdu.title: اردو گرامر — اسم، فعل، صفت

Urdu.body: مترادف الفاظ وہ ہیں جن کے معنی ایک جیسے ہوں، جیسے خوش = مسرور، بہادر = دلیر، امیر = دولت مند، سچ = حق۔ متضاد الفاظ وہ ہیں جن کے معنی الٹ ہوں، جیسے دن ≠ رات، اچھا ≠ برا، امیر ≠ غریب، سچ ≠ جھوٹ، روشنی ≠ اندھیرا۔ امتحان میں مترادف/متضاد کے سوالات میں چاروں آپشن پڑھ کر درست جواب چنیں، کیونکہ قریب المعنی الفاظ دھوکہ دے سکتے ہیں۔ روزانہ دس نئے الفاظ یاد کرنا بہترین طریقہ ہے۔
Urdu.title: مترادف اور متضاد الفاظ

Urdu.body: اردو میں واحد سے جمع بنانے کے کئی طریقے ہیں: کتاب سے کتابیں، لڑکا سے لڑکے، استاد سے اساتذہ، خبر سے اخبار، مسجد سے مساجد، دوست سے دوستوں۔ مذکر سے مونث بنانے کے لیے اکثر 'ی' یا 'ہ' کا اضافہ ہوتا ہے: لڑکا سے لڑکی، استاد سے استانی، شیر سے شیرنی، مرغا سے مرغی۔ کچھ الفاظ کے مذکر مونث یاد رکھنے پڑتے ہیں، جیسے ابا/اماں، باپ/ماں، بھائی/بہن۔ امتحان میں عربی اور فارسی کے الفاظ کی جمع بھی پوچھی جاتی ہے۔
Urdu.title: واحد جمع اور مذکر مونث

Urdu.body: محاورہ وہ جملہ یا الفاظ کا مجموعہ ہے جس کا مطلب لفظی معنی سے مختلف ہو، جیسے 'آنکھوں کا تارا' یعنی بہت پیارا، 'باغ باغ ہونا' یعنی بہت خوش ہونا، 'ناک میں دم کرنا' یعنی بہت تنگ کرنا۔ ضرب المثل ایک مکمل جملہ ہوتا ہے جس میں تجربے کی بات ہو، جیسے 'جیسا کرو گے ویسا بھرو گے' اور 'خالی برتن زیادہ بجتا ہے'۔ امتحان میں محاورے کا مطلب یا اس کا درست استعمال پوچھا جاتا ہے۔ محاوروں کو جملوں میں استعمال کر کے یاد کریں۔
Urdu.title: محاورے اور ضرب الامثال

Urdu.body: میر تقی میر کو 'خدائے سخن' کہا جاتا ہے؛ غالب (مرزا اسد اللہ خان غالب) اردو کے سب سے بڑے شاعر مانے جاتے ہیں۔ علامہ اقبال 'شاعر مشرق' ہیں اور ان کی مشہور کتابیں بانگ درا، بال جبریل اور ضرب کلیم ہیں۔ احمد فراز، فیض احمد فیض اور جون ایلیا جدید اردو شاعری کے بڑے نام ہیں۔ اردو نثر میں سر سید احمد خان، مولانا حالی اور پطرس بخاری مشہور ہیں۔ امتحان میں شاعر کا لقب یا کتاب کا مصنف پوچھا جاتا ہے۔
Urdu.title: اردو ادب — مشہور شعرا و ادبا

Urdu.body: حروف وہ الفاظ ہیں جو دو الفاظ یا جملوں کو جوڑتے ہیں، جیسے کا، کی، کے، سے، میں، پر، اور، لیکن، اگر۔ جملہ اسمیہ وہ ہے جس میں فعل نہ ہو، جیسے 'علی اچھا لڑکا ہے'۔ جملہ فعلیہ وہ ہے جس میں فعل ہو، جیسے 'علی کتاب پڑھتا ہے'۔ جملہ خبریہ خبر دیتا ہے، جملہ استفہامیہ سوال پوچھتا ہے، جملہ امریہ حکم دیتا ہے۔ 'نے' کا استعمال ماضی میں فاعل کے ساتھ ہوتا ہے، جیسے 'علی نے کتاب پڑھی'۔
Urdu.title: حروف اور جملے کی اقسام

Tajweed.body: Makharij are the places in the mouth and throat from which Arabic letters are pronounced. There are 5 general places (Makharij Aammah): the throat (Halq), the tongue (Lisan), the lips (Shafatan), the nasal passage (Khayshoom) and the empty space of the mouth (Jawf). These divide into 17 detailed places (Makharij Khaassah). Correct Makhraj is the foundation of Tajweed — a letter pronounced from the wrong place changes its sound and sometimes its meaning.
Tajweed.title: Makharij — The Places of Articulation

Tajweed.body: Jawf (empty mouth space): the Madd letters Alif, Waw and Ya when they are Madd. Halq (throat): six letters — Hamza and Ha from the deepest part, Ain and Ha from the middle, Ghain and Kha from the top. Lisan (tongue): the most letters, including Qaf, Kaf, Jeem, Sheen, Ya, Dad, Lam, Noon, Ra, Ta, Dal, Tha, Seen, Sad, Za. Shafatan (lips): Fa, Ba, Meem, Waw. Khayshoom (nose): Ghunnah, the nasal sound of Noon and Meem.
Tajweed.title: The Five General Makharij in Detail

Tajweed.body: Sifaat are the qualities that distinguish letters sharing the same Makhraj. Key pairs: Hams (whispering, breath flows) vs Jahr (no breath flow); Shiddah (sound stops) vs Rakhawah (sound flows); Isti'la (tongue raised, heavy letters) vs Istifal (light letters). The seven heavy (Mufakhkhamah) letters are Kha, Sad, Dad, Ghain, Ta, Qaf and Za — remembered as 'Khussadaghtin Qiz'. The remaining letters are light (Muraqqaqah). Ra is heavy or light depending on its vowel.
Tajweed.title: Sifaat — The Qualities of Letters

Tajweed.body: When Noon Sakinah or Tanween is followed by another letter, one of four rules applies. Izhar (clear): before the six throat letters (Hamza, Ha, Ain, Ha, Ghain, Kha), pronounce the Noon clearly. Idgham (merging): before Yarmaloon letters (Ya, Ra, Meem, Lam, Waw, Noon), merge the Noon into the next letter. Iqlab (conversion): before Ba, change the Noon sound to Meem with Ghunnah. Ikhfa (hiding): before the remaining 15 letters, hide the Noon with a nasal sound (Ghunnah) for two counts.
Tajweed.title: Noon Sakinah and Tanween — Four Rules

Tajweed.body: Meem Sakinah has three rules. Ikhfa Shafawi (lip hiding): when Meem Sakinah is followed by Ba, hide it with Ghunnah, e.g. 'tarmeehim bi-hijarah'. Idgham Shafawi (lip merging): when followed by another Meem, merge the two Meems with Ghunnah. Izhar Shafawi (lip clarity): before all other letters, pronounce the Meem clearly — be careful before Waw and Fa so the Meem is not hidden by mistake. Remember: Meem rules are like Noon rules but simpler — only three.
Tajweed.title: Meem Sakinah — Three Rules

Tajweed.body: Madd means stretching a sound. Madd Tabee'i (natural Madd) is two counts (two Harakat) and occurs when a Madd letter (Alif after Fatha, Waw after Damma, Ya after Kasra) has no Hamza or Sukoon after it. Madd Munfasil (separate) is when the Madd letter is at the end of a word and Hamza begins the next word — stretched 4 or 5 counts. Madd Muttasil (joined) is when the Madd letter and Hamza are in the same word — 4 or 5 counts. Madd Lazim (necessary) is six counts, when a Madd letter is followed by a permanent Sukoon.
Tajweed.title: Madd — Lengthening the Sound

Tajweed.body: Waqf means stopping at the end of a word or verse while reciting. A stop on a word ending in Fatha, Damma or Kasra is made with Sukoon (the vowel is dropped), e.g. 'Alhamdu' becomes 'Alhamd'. A word ending in Tanween Fathatain is stopped with Alif (Madd Iwad), e.g. 'aleeman' becomes 'aleemaa'. Never stop in the middle of a phrase in a way that changes the meaning. Stopping at the end of a verse is always allowed; stopping in the middle requires care about the meaning. The small signs in the Mushaf guide where to stop or continue.
Tajweed.title: Waqf — Rules of Stopping

Tajweed.body: The Quran has 114 Surahs, 30 Parahs and more than 6,200 verses. The first Surah revealed was Al-Alaq (first five verses); the first complete Surah revealed was Al-Fatiha. Surah At-Tawbah is the only Surah without Bismillah at the start. Surah An-Naml contains two Bismillahs. The longest Surah is Al-Baqarah; the shortest is Al-Kausar. Ayat-ul-Kursi (verse 255 of Surah Al-Baqarah) is the greatest verse of the Quran. The Quran was compiled in book form under Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA) and standardised under Hazrat Usman (RA).
Tajweed.title: Quranic Knowledge — Structure and Firsts
Ikhfa — Hiding the Noon Sound (إخفاء)
Tajweed.body: Ikhfa means hiding. When a still Noon (Noon Sakinah) or a Tanween is followed by one of 15 letters — ت ث ج د ذ ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ف ق ك — the Noon sound is neither said out clearly nor merged away completely: it sits in between, held with a nasal hum called Ghunnah for about two counts. The tongue does not press fully into the Noon position; it moves toward the position of the next letter. Before the heavy letters (ص ض ط ظ ق) the nasal sound comes out heavy; before the other ten it stays light. Ikhfa Shafawi is the lip version: a still Meem followed only by Ba (ب) is hidden with Ghunnah for two counts. Common mistake: saying the Noon clearly, or merging it fully — both miss the in-between sound. Ikhfa is one of the four rules that govern Noon Sakinah and Tanween. Recall first: cover this note and list the 15 Ikhfa letters and the one letter that triggers Ikhfa Shafawi.
Tajweed.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Riyad al-Quran
Tajweed.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — Qari: Tajweed/Hifz + Islamiyat section (30 combined)

Tajweed.title: Idgham — Merging into the Next Letter (إدغام)
Tajweed.body: Idgham means merging: one sound is inserted into the next so that two sounds are heard as one doubled sound. It applies to Noon Sakinah or Tanween followed by six letters, remembered by the word يَرْمَلُون (Ya, Ra, Meem, Lam, Waw, Noon). With Ghunnah (nasal sound, two counts): Ya, Noon, Meem and Waw — remembered as يَنْمُو. Without Ghunnah (no nasal sound at all): Lam and Ra only. The merged letter sounds doubled, as if it carried a Shaddah. Idgham happens only across two separate words: if the Noon and the trigger letter are inside one word, the Noon is said clearly instead. Idgham Shafawi is the Meem version: a still Meem followed by another Meem merges into one doubled Meem with Ghunnah for two counts. Recall first: cover this note and name the six Idgham letters and the two that carry no Ghunnah.
Tajweed.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Riwaq Al Quran
Tajweed.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — Qari: Tajweed/Hifz + Islamiyat section (30 combined)

Tajweed.title: Qalqalah — The Echo Letters (قلقلة)
Tajweed.body: Qalqalah means shaking or disturbance: a short bounce or echo is heard on the letter. It applies only to five letters, remembered by the phrase قُطْبُ جَدٍّ (Qaf, Ta, Ba, Jeem, Dal). It happens only when one of these letters has no vowel (Sukoon), or when stopping on it creates a Sukoon. Qalqalah Sughra (minor) is the lightest bounce, when the letter has its own Sukoon in the middle of a word and reading continues. Qalqalah Kubra (major) is a stronger bounce, when the reader stops on a word ending in a Qalqalah letter. Some books add a strongest level for stopping on a Qalqalah letter that also carries a Shaddah; others count that as part of Kubra — the letters are the same either way. Common mistake: turning the bounce into a full vowel sound (Fatha, Kasra or Damma). Recall first: cover this note and list the five Qalqalah letters and when the bounce is strongest.
Tajweed.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — Qari: Tajweed/Hifz + Islamiyat section (30 combined)

Tajweed.title: Madd Types Compared — How Long to Stretch (مد)
Tajweed.body: Madd means stretching a vowel sound. The three Madd letters are Alif, Waw and Ya. One count (Harakah) is roughly the time of one short vowel; length is judged by steady rhythm, not by clock seconds. Madd Tabi'i (natural, also called Madd Asli) is the basic form, with no Hamzah or Sukoon after it — always two counts. Madd Muttasil (connected) is a Madd letter followed by Hamzah in the same word — four or five counts. Madd Munfasil (separate) is a Madd letter at the end of one word with Hamzah starting the next word — its counts vary by reading route, commonly four or five in the Hafs route. Madd Lazim (necessary) is a Madd letter followed by a permanent Sukoon or a Shaddah — always six counts, the longest fixed Madd. Madd Badal (substitute) is Hamzah coming before the Madd letter — two counts. Madd Arid lis-Sukun is when stopping makes the letter after a Madd letter temporarily still — two, four or six counts, the reader's choice. Recall first: cover this note and match each Madd type to its counts.
Tajweed.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Hekma Academy
Tajweed.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — Qari: Tajweed/Hifz + Islamiyat section (30 combined)

Tajweed.title: Iqlab — Turning Noon into Meem (إقلاب)
Tajweed.body: Iqlab means conversion. It is the rarest of the four Noon Sakinah rules because it has only one trigger letter: Ba (ب). When Noon Sakinah or Tanween is followed by Ba, the Noon sound turns into a hidden Meem sound, held with Ghunnah for two counts. The lips come together as for Meem, but the sound stays soft and nasal — it is not a clear Meem. Together the four rules cover the whole alphabet: Izhar 6 letters, Idgham 6 letters, Iqlab 1 letter and Ikhfa 15 letters — 6 + 6 + 1 + 15 = 28. Common mistake: saying the Noon clearly before Ba, or skipping the Ghunnah. Recall first: cover this note and say which single letter triggers Iqlab and what the Noon turns into.
Tajweed.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Al-Wafa Institute
Tajweed.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — Qari: Tajweed/Hifz + Islamiyat section (30 combined)

Tajweed.title: Common Tajweed Mistakes to Avoid
Tajweed.body: Six mistakes show up again and again in practice. (1) Saying the Noon clearly before an Ikhfa letter — Ikhfa is a hidden sound with Ghunnah, not a clear Noon. (2) Merging the Noon fully before an Ikhfa letter — Ikhfa is in between clear and merged. (3) Applying Idgham inside a single word — Idgham only happens across two words. (4) Turning Qalqalah into a full vowel — the bounce is a short echo, not Fatha, Kasra or Damma. (5) Stretching Madd by guesswork — Madd Tabi'i is two counts, Madd Lazim is six, and the others have fixed counts; count them steadily. (6) Hiding a clear Meem by accident before Waw and Fa — Izhar Shafawi needs extra care there, because the lips are already close to the Meem position. Recall first: cover this note and explain why each of the six is a mistake.
Tajweed.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — Qari: Tajweed/Hifz + Islamiyat section (30 combined)

Tajweed.title: Sifaat in Detail — Hams, Jahr, Shiddah and Rakhawah
Tajweed.body: Sifaat are the qualities that tell apart letters sharing one Makhraj. Hams means breath flows with the letter — ten letters carry it. Jahr means the breath does not flow — the rest carry it. Shiddah means the sound stops and is held back — eight letters carry it. Rakhawah means the sound flows. Between them sits Tawassut, the middle quality, carried by five letters: Laam, Noon, Ayn, Meem and Raa. Isti'la raises the tongue and makes seven letters heavy; Istifal leaves the rest light. Itbaq presses the tongue towards the palate for four letters: Saad, Daad, Taa and Zaa. Idhlaq makes six letters light and quick on the tongue: Faa, Raa, Meem, Noon, Laam and Baa. Roman Urdu: Sifaat harf ki khoobiyan hain; Hams mein saans behti hai, Shiddah mein awaz rukti hai. Recall first: cover this note and pair each quality with its opposite and its count where given.
