Tajweed.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Tajweed and Hifz Curriculum
Tajweed.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — Qari: Tajweed/Hifz + Islamiyat block (30)

Tajweed.title: Heavy and Light — Tafkheem, Tarqeeq, Raa and Laam
Tajweed.body: Tafkheem is reading a letter heavily, with the mouth full; Tarqeeq is reading it lightly. The seven Isti'la letters are always heavy. Raa follows its vowel: with a Fatha or a Dammah it is heavy; with a Kasrah it is light. A still Raa usually follows the vowel before it. The Laam in the name of Allah follows the vowel before it too: after a Fatha or a Dammah it is heavy; after a Kasrah it is light. All other Laams are read light. Roman Urdu: Tafkheem ka matlab hai harf ko bhari parhna; Raa zabar ya pesh se bhari, zer se halki hoti hai. Recall first: cover this note and state the Raa rule and the Laam rule in one line each.
Tajweed.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Tajweed and Hifz Curriculum
Tajweed.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — Qari: Tajweed/Hifz + Islamiyat block (30)

Tajweed.title: Sun and Moon Letters — Laam Qamariyyah and Shamsiyyah
Tajweed.body: When 'Al-' meets the next word, its Laam behaves in two ways. Before the fourteen sun letters, the Laam merges into the next letter and is not pronounced — the next letter carries a Shaddah. The sun letters are: Ta, Tha, Dal, Dhal, Ra, Za, Seen, Sheen, Sad, Dad, Ta, Za, Lam and Noon — two different Ta sounds and two different Za sounds both belong here. Before the fourteen moon letters, the Laam is pronounced clearly. The moon letters are: Alif, Ba, Jeem, Ha, Kha, Ain, Ghain, Fa, Qaf, Kaf, Meem, Ha, Waw and Ya — the two Ha sounds, one from the throat and one soft, are both moon letters. The two groups are named after the words for sun and moon. Roman Urdu: shamsi haroof se pehle Laam parha nahi jata; qamari haroof se pehle Laam saaf parha jata hai. Recall first: cover this note and say how many letters are in each group and what happens to the Laam before each.
Tajweed.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Tajweed and Hifz Curriculum
Tajweed.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — Qari: Tajweed/Hifz + Islamiyat block (30)

Tajweed.title: Hamzatul Wasl and Hamzatul Qat'
Tajweed.body: Hamzatul Wasl is a Hamzah that appears at the start of some words, including the 'Al-' prefix. When words are joined in recitation, it is dropped and not pronounced. When starting on that word, it is pronounced. Hamzatul Qat' is different: it is always pronounced, whether starting or joining. Telling them apart matters because dropping a Qat' Hamzah, or pronouncing a Wasl Hamzah in the middle of a phrase, changes the recitation. Roman Urdu: Hamzatul Wasl milane par gir jata hai, shuru mein parha jata hai; Hamzatul Qat' hamesha parha jata hai. Recall first: cover this note and say when each Hamzah is pronounced.
Tajweed.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Tajweed and Hifz Curriculum
Tajweed.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — Qari: Tajweed/Hifz + Islamiyat block (30)

Tajweed.title: More Madd Types — Leen, Iwaz, Silah and Far'i
Tajweed.body: Madd Asli is the natural stretch of two counts with no cause. Madd Far'i is any extra stretch caused by a Hamzah or a Sukoon after the Madd letter. Madd Leen is the soft stretch of a still Waw or Yaa preceded by a Fatha, heard at a stop: two, four or six counts. Madd Iwaz replaces Tanween Fathatain with an Alif at a stop, stretched two counts. Madd Silah lengthens the Haa of the pronoun between two vowels: two counts normally (Silah Sughra), and four or five counts when a Hamzah follows (Silah Kubra). Roman Urdu: Madd Far'i ki wajah Hamzah ya Sukoon hoti hai; Leen, Iwaz aur Silah is ki qismein hain. Recall first: cover this note and define Leen, Iwaz and Silah with their counts.
Tajweed.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Tajweed and Hifz Curriculum
Tajweed.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — Qari: Tajweed/Hifz + Islamiyat block (30)

Tajweed.title: Waqf Signs in the Mushaf — Ja, La, Sali, Qali and Saktah
Tajweed.body: Small signs in the Mushaf guide stopping. Jaa (ج) means stopping is allowed. Laa (لا) means do not stop — the meaning is incomplete. Sali (صلى) means it is better to continue. Qali (قلى) means it is better to stop. Saktah (س) means a brief pause without taking a breath, then continuing. Meem (م) means a required stop. Stops also have grades: Taam is complete, Kaafi is sufficient, Hasan is good, and Qabeeh is a bad stop that distorts the meaning and must be avoided. Roman Urdu: Mushaf ke chhote nishan batate hain ke kahan rukna hai aur kahan nahi. Recall first: cover this note and give the meaning of Jaa, Laa, Sali, Qali and Saktah.
Tajweed.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Tajweed and Hifz Curriculum
Tajweed.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — Qari: Tajweed/Hifz + Islamiyat block (30)

Tajweed.title: Idgham Families — Same, Near and Close Letters
Tajweed.body: Beyond the Noon and Meem rules, Idgham also joins other letters. Mutamathilain is the merging of two identical letters meeting each other: the first melts into the second. Mutajanisain is the merging of two letters from the same place of articulation that differ in quality. Mutaqaribain is the merging of two letters whose places or qualities are near each other. In each case the first letter loses its own sound and the second is strengthened. These families explain why some letter pairs merge smoothly in recitation. Roman Urdu: Idgham ki teen qismein hain — aik jaise, aik Makhraj wale aur qareebi haroof. Recall first: cover this note and define the three Idgham families.
Tajweed.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Tajweed and Hifz Curriculum
Tajweed.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — Qari: Tajweed/Hifz + Islamiyat block (30)

Tajweed.title: Hifz Method — Sabq, Sabqi and Amukhta
Tajweed.body: Hifz study is usually split into three daily parts. Sabq is the new lesson: a small portion memorised for the first time, repeated many times while looking until it can be recited from memory. Sabqi is the revision of recent lessons, usually the last few days of new work, recited to fix them before they fade. Amukhta is the revision of old portions memorised long ago, recited in rotation so nothing is lost. A common day covers all three: new lesson first, then recent revision, then old revision. Roman Urdu: Sabq naya sabaq, Sabqi haal ka dohrao, Amukhta purani manzil ka dohrao hai. Recall first: cover this note and say what each of the three parts covers.
Tajweed.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Tajweed and Hifz Curriculum
Tajweed.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — Qari: Tajweed/Hifz + Islamiyat block (30)

Tajweed.title: Revision Cycles — Keeping What You Memorised
Tajweed.body: Memory fades without review, so Hifz depends on revision cycles. New portions are revised the same day, then again the next days, then weekly, then in longer rotations. Old portions are recited in a fixed rotation — a set number of pages or a set Juz portion each day — so every part returns regularly. Revision comes before new lessons when time is short: protecting old Hifz matters more than adding new pages. Reciting from memory, rather than only reading, is the true test of whether a portion is fixed. Roman Urdu: dohrao ke baghair Hifz kamzor ho jata hai; purani manzil ka dohrao naye sabaq se pehle hai. Recall first: cover this note and explain why revision comes before new lessons when time is short.
Tajweed.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Tajweed and Hifz Curriculum
Tajweed.syllabusClause: Pattern B (ESED-453) — Qari: Tajweed/Hifz + Islamiyat block (30)

Tajweed.title: Listening, a Teacher and One Mushaf — Hifz Supports
Tajweed.body: Three supports strengthen Hifz. Listening to a skilled Qari fixes the words and their Tajweed through the ear, and fills gaps between study sessions. Reciting to a teacher catches small mistakes early, before they become habits; a student should not rely only on self-checking. Using the same Mushaf every day builds visual memory, because the student remembers where each verse sits on the page. Understanding the meaning also helps: it gives the memory hooks to recall and link verses. Many teachers also advise learning new lessons in the early morning, when the mind is fresh, and beginning with the short Surahs of the last Juz. Roman Urdu: sunna, ustad ko sunana aur aik hi Mushaf istemal karna Hifz ko mazboot karte hain. Recall first: cover this note and name three supports for Hifz and what each one does.
Tajweed.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Tajweed and Hifz Curriculum

IT/Computer.body: Microsoft Word is a word-processing program used to write letters, essays and reports. You can change the font, size and colour of text, make headings bold, insert tables and pictures, and check spelling. Files are usually saved with the .docx extension. The ribbon at the top holds the tools (Home, Insert, Layout); the cursor shows where text will appear. Exam tip: Word = writing documents; a word processor is not a spreadsheet. Roman Urdu: Word se dastavezat likhi jati hain — letter, darkhwast, mazmoon. Recall first: cover this note and say what MS Word is used for and what its usual file extension is.
IT/Computer.title: MS Word — Word Processing

IT/Computer.body: Microsoft Excel is a spreadsheet program used for numbers, tables and calculations. Data sits in cells arranged in rows (numbered 1, 2, 3) and columns (lettered A, B, C); a cell address like B5 means column B, row 5. Formulas start with '=' — for example =SUM(A1:A5) adds cells A1 to A5, and =AVERAGE(B1:B10) finds their average. Excel files are usually saved with the .xlsx extension. Exam tip: Excel = numbers and formulas; rows are numbers, columns are letters. Recall first: cover this note and explain what the cell address B5 means and what =SUM(A1:A5) does.
IT/Computer.title: MS Excel — Spreadsheets and Formulas

IT/Computer.body: Microsoft PowerPoint is used to make presentations — a series of slides shown on a screen. Each slide can hold a title, bullet points, pictures, charts and tables. Transitions move from one slide to the next; animations move objects inside a slide. The Slide Show view (F5) plays the presentation full-screen. Files are usually saved with the .pptx extension. Exam tip: PowerPoint = slides for a presentation; Word = documents, Excel = numbers, PowerPoint = slides. Recall first: cover this note and say the difference between a transition and an animation.
IT/Computer.title: MS PowerPoint — Presentations and Slides

IT/Computer.body: Hardware is the physical part of a computer you can touch. The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the brain — it does the processing. RAM is short-term memory: it holds what you are working on now and is cleared when the computer turns off. ROM and the hard disk store data permanently. Input devices put data in: keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone. Output devices show results: monitor, printer, speakers. The motherboard connects all parts together. Roman Urdu: CPU dimagh hai, RAM aarzi yaaddasht hai, hard disk mustaqil zakhira hai. Recall first: cover this note and sort keyboard, mouse, monitor, printer and CPU into input, output and processing.
IT/Computer.title: Computer Hardware — CPU, Memory, Input and Output

IT/Computer.body: The internet is a worldwide network of connected computers. The World Wide Web (WWW) is the system of web pages you visit with a browser such as Chrome or Edge. A website address (URL) starts with http or https — the 's' means the connection is secure. Email sends messages through an address like name@example.com; the @ sign separates the user name from the domain. A search engine (e.g. Google) finds pages; a browser displays them — they are not the same thing. Wi-Fi connects devices to the internet without wires. Recall first: cover this note and explain the difference between a browser and a search engine.
IT/Computer.title: Internet Basics — Web, Browser, Email

IT/Computer.body: Keyboard shortcuts save time in exams and in office work. Ctrl + C = copy, Ctrl + X = cut, Ctrl + V = paste, Ctrl + Z = undo, Ctrl + Y = redo, Ctrl + S = save, Ctrl + A = select all, Ctrl + P = print, Ctrl + F = find, Alt + Tab = switch between open windows, F5 = start a PowerPoint slide show, Ctrl + B = bold, Ctrl + I = italic, Ctrl + U = underline. Learn them as pairs: copy-paste (C, V), undo-redo (Z, Y), save-print (S, P). In a test the question usually gives the shortcut and asks what it does. Recall first: cover this note and say what Ctrl + C, Ctrl + V, Ctrl + Z, Ctrl + S and Alt + Tab do.
IT/Computer.title: Keyboard Shortcuts — The Essential List
Operating Systems — What the OS Does
IT/Computer.body: Every computer needs an operating system (OS): the software that manages the hardware and all other programs. The OS controls memory, organises files, handles input and output, and shows the user interface. Common examples are Microsoft Windows, macOS and Linux. Most systems use a GUI (Graphical User Interface) with windows, icons and menus, plus a desktop and taskbar. Deleted files wait in the Recycle Bin until they are restored or removed for good. Roman Urdu: OS computer ko chalata hai — memory, files aur programs sab is ke control mein hote hain. Recall first: cover this note and name three jobs of an operating system.
IT/Computer.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Computer Fundamentals Curriculum

IT/Computer.title: System Software vs Application Software
IT/Computer.body: System software runs the computer itself: the operating system, drivers that let hardware talk to the computer, and utility programs such as antivirus tools and backup tools. Application software helps the user do a task: MS Word writes documents, Excel handles numbers, browsers open the web, and games entertain. A simple test: if removing it stops the computer working, it is system software; if it only stops one job, it is an application. Roman Urdu: system software computer ko chalata hai, application software kaam karwata hai. Recall first: cover this note and sort OS, Word, antivirus and browser into system or application software.
IT/Computer.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Computer Fundamentals Curriculum

IT/Computer.title: Storage Devices — HDD, SSD, USB and Optical Discs
IT/Computer.body: A hard disk drive (HDD) stores data on spinning magnetic discs; it is cheap and roomy but has moving parts. A solid state drive (SSD) uses flash memory with no moving parts, so it is faster and tougher. A USB flash drive is small, portable flash storage. CDs and DVDs are optical discs read by a laser. Sizes grow as kilobyte (KB), megabyte (MB), gigabyte (GB) and terabyte (TB); 1 GB equals 1,024 MB. Roman Urdu: HDD ghoomta hai, SSD mein koi harkat wala hissa nahi — is liye SSD tez hoti hai. Recall first: cover this note and order KB, MB, GB and TB, and say how a CD is read.
IT/Computer.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Computer Fundamentals Curriculum

IT/Computer.title: Computer Hardware — Printers, Scanners and Ports
IT/Computer.body: An inkjet printer sprays tiny drops of ink and suits home use; a laser printer uses toner powder and suits large, fast print jobs. A scanner turns paper pages and photos into digital files. The monitor, also called a VDU (Visual Display Unit), shows output. Keyboards, mice and flash drives usually connect through USB (Universal Serial Bus) ports. Function keys (F1–F12) give quick commands, such as F1 for help. Roman Urdu: inkjet siyahi chhidakta hai, laser toner istemal karta hai. Recall first: cover this note and say which printer uses toner and what USB stands for.
IT/Computer.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Computer Fundamentals Curriculum

IT/Computer.title: Files and Folders — Organising Your Work
IT/Computer.body: Files hold work (documents, pictures, music) and folders organise them, like drawers in a cabinet. The file extension shows the kind of file: .docx for Word, .txt for plain text, .pdf for portable documents, .jpg for pictures and .mp3 for audio. 'Save' keeps changes in the same file; 'Save As' stores a copy under a new name or in a new folder. Deleted files wait in the Recycle Bin and can be restored. Roman Urdu: file kaam rakhti hai, folder files ko tartib deta hai. Recall first: cover this note and match .pdf, .jpg and .mp3 to document, picture and audio.
IT/Computer.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Computer Fundamentals Curriculum

IT/Computer.title: MS Word — Formatting and Editing
IT/Computer.body: MS Word is a word processor for letters, essays and reports. Ctrl + B makes text bold, Ctrl + I italic and Ctrl + U underlined; Ctrl + A selects everything. Text can be aligned left, centre or right, and the font and size can be changed from the Home tab. F7 runs the spell check. Word files usually end in .docx. The ribbon at the top holds the tools, and the cursor shows where typing will appear. Roman Urdu: Word se dastavezat likhte hain; Ctrl + B mota, Ctrl + I tedha karta hai. Recall first: cover this note and name the shortcuts for bold, select-all and spell check.
IT/Computer.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Computer Fundamentals Curriculum

IT/Computer.title: MS Excel — Functions and Cell Addresses
IT/Computer.body: MS Excel is a spreadsheet program: a workbook holds worksheets, and each worksheet is a grid of rows and columns. A cell address names the column letter first and the row number second — B5 is column B, row 5. Every formula starts with =. SUM adds numbers, AVERAGE finds the mean, MAX finds the largest and MIN the smallest. Results update automatically when the numbers change. Roman Urdu: Excel mein hisab hota hai; har formula = se shuru hota hai. Recall first: cover this note and say what B5 means and which function finds the average.
IT/Computer.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Computer Fundamentals Curriculum

IT/Computer.title: MS PowerPoint — Building a Slideshow
IT/Computer.body: MS PowerPoint makes slideshows: each slide is one page of the presentation, holding text, pictures or charts. A layout arranges the title and content boxes on a slide. F5 starts the show from the first slide; Shift + F5 starts from the current slide. Keep slides short — a few clear points per slide, with large text the audience can read. Presentations are usually saved as .pptx files. Roman Urdu: PowerPoint se slideshow banti hai; F5 se show pehli slide se shuru hota hai. Recall first: cover this note and say what F5 does and what a layout arranges.
IT/Computer.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Computer Fundamentals Curriculum

IT/Computer.title: Internet and Email — URLs, Browsers and Messages
IT/Computer.body: The internet links computers around the world; the web is the system of pages reached through it. A browser (such as Chrome or Firefox) opens pages; a search engine (such as Google) finds them. A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is a page's address, and HTTPS is the secure, encrypted version of HTTP. An email needs a recipient address with @, a subject line, and can carry attachments; CC sends a copy to extra people. Downloading brings a file to your computer; uploading sends it away. Roman Urdu: browser page kholta hai, search engine dhoondta hai. Recall first: cover this note and explain URL, CC and the difference between download and upload.
IT/Computer.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Computer Fundamentals Curriculum

IT/Computer.title: Staying Safe on a Computer
IT/Computer.body: Good security starts with a strong password: long, with upper-case and lower-case letters, numbers and symbols, and different for each account. Phishing messages pretend to come from a trusted sender to steal passwords — never open their links or attachments. Antivirus software guards against viruses; keep it updated. Keep a backup — a spare copy of important files on another drive or in the cloud — so work survives damage, theft or deletion. Roman Urdu: mazboot password lamba aur mukhtalif hota hai; phishing se hoshiyar rahen. Recall first: cover this note and name three parts of staying safe: password, phishing and backup.
IT/Computer.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Computer Fundamentals Curriculum

IT/Computer.title: Binary — How Computers Count
IT/Computer.body: Computers store everything as binary digits: 0 and 1. One binary digit is a BIT (Binary Digit), and 8 bits make 1 byte. A byte can hold one character, such as a letter. This is why storage sizes step by 1,024: 1 KB is 1,024 bytes, 1 MB is 1,024 KB and 1 GB is 1,024 MB. Desktops, laptops and tablets all work the same way inside — they differ mainly in size and portability. Roman Urdu: computer sirf 0 aur 1 samajhta hai; 8 bit se 1 byte banta hai. Recall first: cover this note and say what BIT stands for and how many bits make a byte.
IT/Computer.source: Original content — concept-extracted from Standard Computer Fundamentals Curriculum

English.body: 'A' is used before a consonant sound (a book, a university — 'university' starts with a 'yoo' sound), 'an' before a vowel sound (an hour, an honest man — the 'h' is silent). 'The' is used for a specific or already-known thing, for unique things (the sun, the Quran), and for rivers, seas and mountain ranges (the Indus, the Himalayas). No article is used before most proper names, languages or games (Ali, Urdu, cricket). Exam tip: choose by sound, not by the first letter.
English.title: Articles — A, An, The

English.body: Learn prepositions with their verbs and adjectives: good at, interested in, afraid of, famous for, depend on, believe in, listen to, look after, deal with, consist of, accused of, capable of. 'In' is used for months, years and long periods (in June, in 2025); 'on' for days and dates (on Monday, on 14 August); 'at' for exact times (at 9 o'clock). 'Between' is for two things, 'among' for more than two. Avoid guessing — memorise the fixed pairs.
English.title: Prepositions — Common Fixed Pairs

English.body: In active voice the subject does the action (Ali wrote the letter); in passive voice the subject receives it (The letter was written by Ali). To change to passive, make the object the subject, use a form of 'be' + past participle, and add 'by' + the doer if needed. Present simple: 'He writes a letter' becomes 'A letter is written by him'. Past simple: 'She cleaned the room' becomes 'The room was cleaned by her'. Note: intransitive verbs (sleep, go, arrive) have no passive form.
English.title: Active and Passive Voice

English.body: In indirect speech, the reporting verb tense usually shifts back: present simple becomes past simple, 'will' becomes 'would', 'can' becomes 'could'. Pronouns and time words change too: 'today' becomes 'that day', 'now' becomes 'then', 'here' becomes 'there', 'this' becomes 'that'. A statement uses 'that' (He said that he was busy); a yes/no question uses 'if' or 'whether' (He asked if I was ready); a wh-question keeps the wh-word (She asked where I lived). Commands become 'told/asked + to + verb'.
English.title: Direct and Indirect Narration

English.body: A singular subject takes a singular verb (He plays; She teaches) and a plural subject takes a plural verb (They play). 'Each', 'every', 'either', 'neither' and 'everyone' are singular (Everyone is here). With 'either...or' and 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject (Neither the students nor the teacher was present). Words like 'news', 'mathematics' and 'physics' look plural but take singular verbs. Collective nouns like 'team' usually take a singular verb when acting as one unit.
English.title: Subject-Verb Agreement

English.body: Learn pairs, not single words. Brave = courageous (antonym: cowardly); honest = truthful (antonym: dishonest); happy = glad (antonym: sad); generous = liberal (antonym: miserly); ancient = old (antonym: modern); victory = triumph (antonym: defeat); abundant = plentiful (antonym: scarce); transparent = clear (antonym: opaque). In the test, read all four options before choosing — a near-synonym can be a trap when the exact match is also present.
English.title: Synonyms and Antonyms — High-Frequency Words

English.body: Present simple: habits and facts (She teaches daily). Present continuous: action in progress (She is teaching now). Past simple: finished past action (He came yesterday). Present perfect: past action with present result (I have finished my work). Past perfect: earlier of two past actions (He had left before I arrived). Future simple: 'will' + verb (I will come tomorrow). For 'since' use perfect tenses (I have lived here since 2020); for 'for' + duration, also perfect tenses (for five years).
English.title: Tenses — Quick Map

English.body: Watch for these frequent errors: 'He is good in English' is wrong — say 'good at English'. 'Discuss about the matter' is wrong — say 'discuss the matter'. 'One of the boys are' is wrong — say 'one of the boys is'. 'Neither of them are' is wrong — say 'neither of them is'. 'I have been living here since five years' is wrong — use 'for five years'. 'The teacher asked to me' is wrong — say 'asked me'. In correction MCQs, check the verb, the preposition and the article first.
English.title: Sentence Correction — Common Errors

Social Studies.body: The Pakistan Movement grew from the Two-Nation Theory — the idea that Muslims and Hindus were two separate nations. The Muslim League was founded in Dhaka in 1906. The Lahore Resolution of 23 March 1940 demanded separate states for the Muslims. In 1946 the Cabinet Mission came from Britain with a plan for India's future; the League first accepted it and then rejected it when the Congress's interpretation differed, and the demand for a separate Pakistan hardened. The 1945-46 elections gave the League a sweeping victory in Muslim seats, proving its claim to speak for Muslims. Pakistan came into being on 14 August 1947. Note: the basic milestones are also covered in the Pak Studies notes — this note adds the Cabinet Mission and the 1945-46 elections. Recall first: cover this note and explain the role of the Cabinet Mission (1946) and the 1945-46 elections in the Pakistan Movement.
Social Studies.title: Pakistan Movement — Cabinet Mission and the 1945-46 Elections

Social Studies.body: The 1973 Constitution is Pakistan's current constitution. It was passed on 10 April 1973 and came into force on 14 August 1973. Beyond its basic structure (Islamic Republic, parliamentary system, bicameral legislature), two parts are asked most: fundamental rights — the constitution guarantees rights such as equality before law, freedom of speech, freedom of religion and the right to education; and the 18th Amendment of 2010, which gave the provinces greater autonomy and abolished the concurrent legislative list. It is Pakistan's longest-serving constitution. Note: the basic facts are also in the Pak Studies notes — this note adds fundamental rights and the 18th Amendment. Recall first: cover this note and name three fundamental rights in the 1973 Constitution and what the 18th Amendment did.
Social Studies.title: 1973 Constitution — Fundamental Rights and the 18th Amendment

Social Studies.body: Gandhara was an ancient civilisation in the north-west of the subcontinent — the area of present-day Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and northern Punjab, with Taxila as its great centre of learning. It flourished under the Mauryan emperor Ashoka and later under the Kushan king Kanishka. Gandhara is famous for its Greco-Buddhist art — Buddha statues carved in a Greek style — and for the university of Taxila, where students from many lands came to study. Its remains at Taxila and Takht-i-Bahi are now UNESCO World Heritage Sites. For the test, remember: Gandhara = KP region, Taxila, Buddhist art, Kanishka. Recall first: cover this note and say where Gandhara was, what its art is called, and which king it flourished under.
Social Studies.title: Gandhara Civilisation — Taxila and Greco-Buddhist Art

Social Studies.body: The geography of Pakistan in one picture: the country lies between the mountains of the north (Karakoram, Himalayas, Hindu Kush — K2, 8,611 m, is the second-highest mountain in the world) and the Arabian Sea in the south. The Indus and its tributaries water the plains of Punjab and Sindh. The main deserts are the Thar in Sindh and the Cholistan in Punjab. The main seaport is Karachi; Gwadar in Balochistan is the deep-sea port. The Khyber Pass connects Peshawar to Afghanistan. Balochistan is the largest province by area; Punjab is the most populous. Note: rivers and dams are covered in more detail in the GK notes. Recall first: cover this note and name the two main deserts, the two main ports and the pass that connects Peshawar to Afghanistan.
Social Studies.title: Geography of Pakistan — Mountains, Deserts, Ports and Passes

flashcards.back: Eight stages across life; key school stages: Initiative vs Guilt, Industry vs Inferiority (6–12 years), Identity vs Role Confusion (adolescence).
flashcards.front: What are Erik Erikson's stages of psychosocial development?

flashcards.back: Students learn together in pairs or groups — think-pair-share, group projects, peer tutoring — building understanding and communication.
flashcards.front: What is collaborative learning?

flashcards.back: Visual (pictures, diagrams), auditory (listening, discussion) and kinaesthetic (doing, moving, hands-on). Good teaching uses a mix of all three.
flashcards.front: Name the three main learning styles.

flashcards.back: A clear objective, a starter, main teaching, guided and independent practice, and a closing with assessment; objectives should be SMART.
flashcards.front: What are the main parts of a good lesson plan?

flashcards.back: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.
flashcards.front: What does SMART mean for lesson objectives?

flashcards.back: A teacher's belief about what students can achieve influences how students actually perform — high expectations tend to raise achievement.
flashcards.front: What is the Pygmalion effect (teacher expectation effect)?

flashcards.back: Giving the learner a little more than their current level (input + 1), so new language is slightly challenging but understandable.
flashcards.front: What is Krashen's 'i + 1' in language learning?

flashcards.back: Learning by watching others — attention, retention, reproduction and motivation are the four steps (Bandura).
flashcards.front: What is observational (social) learning?

flashcards.back: Positive reinforcement adds something pleasant to increase a behaviour; negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant to increase a behaviour; punishment decreases a behaviour.
flashcards.front: What is the difference between reinforcement and punishment?

flashcards.back: When a learner connects new information to what they already know, and organises it into existing mental structures (schemas).
flashcards.front: What is meaningful learning (Ausubel)?

flashcards.back: The places of articulation of Arabic letters: 5 general (Jawf, Halq, Lisan, Shafatan, Khayshoom) and 17 detailed places.
flashcards.front: What are Makharij, and how many are there?

flashcards.back: Jawf (empty mouth space), Halq (throat), Lisan (tongue), Shafatan (lips), Khayshoom (nasal passage).
flashcards.front: Name the five general Makharij (Makharij Aammah).

flashcards.back: Sifaat are the qualities of letters, e.g. Hams vs Jahr, Shiddah vs Rakhawah, Isti'la (heavy) vs Istifal (light).
flashcards.front: What are Sifaat in Tajweed?

flashcards.back: Kha, Sad, Dad, Ghain, Ta, Qaf, Za — remembered as 'Khussadaghtin Qiz'. All other letters are light (Muraqqaqah).
flashcards.front: Which seven letters are always heavy (Mufakhkhamah)?

flashcards.back: Four rules: Izhar (clear), Idgham (merging), Iqlab (conversion) and Ikhfa (hiding).
flashcards.front: What are the four rules of Noon Sakinah and Tanween?

flashcards.back: Before the six throat letters: Hamza, Ha, Ain, Ha, Ghain, Kha — pronounce the Noon clearly, with no Ghunnah.
flashcards.front: When does Izhar apply to Noon Sakinah?

flashcards.back: Before the letters of Yarmaloon (Ya, Ra, Meem, Lam, Waw, Noon), the Noon merges into the next letter.
flashcards.front: When does Idgham apply to Noon Sakinah?

flashcards.back: Before Ba, the Noon sound changes to a Meem sound with Ghunnah.
flashcards.front: What is Iqlab, and when does it happen?

flashcards.back: Three rules: Ikhfa Shafawi (before Ba, hidden with Ghunnah), Idgham Shafawi (before Meem, merged) and Izhar Shafawi (before all other letters, clear).
flashcards.front: What are the three rules of Meem Sakinah?

flashcards.back: Madd Tabee'i (natural, 2 counts), Madd Munfasil (separate, 4–5 counts), Madd Muttasil (joined, 4–5 counts), Madd Lazim (necessary, 6 counts).
flashcards.front: Name the main types of Madd and their lengths.

flashcards.back: The nasal sound made in the nose (Khayshoom), heard in Noon and Meem, usually held for two counts in Ikhfa, Idgham and Iqlab.
flashcards.front: What is Ghunnah?

flashcards.back: Stop with Sukoon on a word ending in a vowel; stop with Alif (Madd Iwad) on a word ending in Tanween Fathatain.
flashcards.front: What are the basic rules of Waqf (stopping)?

flashcards.back: 571 AD
flashcards.front: In which year was the Prophet Muhammad (SAW) born?

flashcards.back: 610 AD, in Cave Hira — the first five verses of Surah Al-Alaq.
flashcards.front: When and where was the first revelation?

flashcards.back: 622 AD — the start of the Islamic (Hijri) calendar.
flashcards.front: In which year did the Hijrat (migration to Madinah) take place?

flashcards.back: 2 AH — 313 Muslims against about 1000 Quraish.
flashcards.front: In which Hijri year was the Battle of Badr fought?

flashcards.back: 3 AH
flashcards.front: In which Hijri year was the Battle of Uhud fought?

flashcards.back: 5 AH — a trench was dug around Madinah on the advice of Salman Farsi (RA).
flashcards.front: In which Hijri year was the Battle of Khandaq (the Trench) fought?

flashcards.back: 8 AH
flashcards.front: In which Hijri year was Makkah conquered (Fatah Makkah)?

flashcards.back: 11 AH, in Madinah.
flashcards.front: In which Hijri year did the Prophet Muhammad (SAW) pass away?

flashcards.back: 23 March 1940 — the Lahore Resolution was passed.
flashcards.front: When was the Lahore Resolution passed?

flashcards.back: 14 August 1947
flashcards.front: When did Pakistan come into being?

flashcards.back: 25 December 1876, in Karachi.
flashcards.front: When and where was Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah born?

flashcards.back: 11 September 1948
flashcards.front: When did Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah pass away?

flashcards.back: Nahw studies how words join into sentences and their case endings; Sarf studies how words themselves are built from roots.
flashcards.front: What is the difference between Nahw and Sarf?

flashcards.back: Ism is a noun (person, place, thing); Fi'l is a verb (action with time); Harf is a particle with no complete meaning alone.
flashcards.front: Name the three types of Arabic words and give one example of each.

flashcards.back: Marfu' (nominative) — damma; Mansub (accusative) — fatha; Majrur (genitive) — kasra.
flashcards.front: Match the three i'rab cases to their vowel signs: Marfu', Mansub, Majrur.

flashcards.back: Mubtada' (the subject) + Khabar (the news about it). Example: اَلْكِتَابُ جَدِيدٌ — al-Kitabu is the Mubtada', jadeedun is the Khabar.
flashcards.front: What are the two parts of a nominal sentence (Jumlah Ismiyyah)?

flashcards.back: Fi'l (verb) + Fa'il (doer, Marfu') + Maf'ul bihi (object, Mansub). Order is usually verb-subject-object.
flashcards.front: What are the parts of a verbal sentence (Jumlah Fi'liyyah), in order?

flashcards.back: ك-ت-ب (k-t-b), about writing: كِتَاب (book), كَاتِب (writer), مَكْتُوب (written), مَكْتَبَة (library).
flashcards.front: Give the root of كِتَاب (book) and three other words from the same root.

flashcards.back: هَذَا (this, masculine), هَذِهِ (this, feminine), ذَلِكَ (that, masculine), تِلْكَ (that, feminine).
flashcards.front: What are the Arabic words for 'this' and 'that' (masculine and feminine)?

flashcards.back: Madi (past/perfective, e.g. كَتَبَ — he wrote) and Mudari' (present/future/imperfective, e.g. يَكْتُبُ — he writes).
flashcards.front: What are the two main Arabic verb tenses, and what does each mean?

flashcards.back: Singular (one), dual (exactly two, adds انِ/ينِ, e.g. كِتَابَانِ) and plural (three or more).
flashcards.front: How many numbers does an Arabic noun have, and what does the dual mean?

flashcards.back: Huruf al-Jarr are prepositions such as فِي (in), مِنْ (from), إِلَى (to), عَلَى (on); the noun after them is Majrur (kasra).
flashcards.front: What are Huruf al-Jarr, and what case does the noun after them take?

flashcards.back: Vitamin A — night blindness; Vitamin B1 — beriberi; Vitamin C — scurvy; Vitamin D — rickets.
flashcards.front: Match vitamins A, B1, C and D to their deficiency diseases.

flashcards.back: Kwashiorkor — swollen belly, thin limbs, too little protein; Marasmus — total wasting, too little protein and energy.
flashcards.front: What is the difference between kwashiorkor and marasmus?

flashcards.back: Skeletal muscle (attached to bones, voluntary), smooth muscle (stomach, intestines, blood vessels, involuntary) and cardiac muscle (heart only).
flashcards.front: Name the three types of muscle and where each is found.

flashcards.back: Carbon dioxide + water → (sunlight, chlorophyll) → glucose + oxygen.
flashcards.front: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.

flashcards.back: Roots absorb water and minerals; stem supports and transports; leaves make food; flowers reproduce and make seeds.
flashcards.front: What is the main job of the root, stem, leaf and flower of a plant?

flashcards.back: Solid (fixed shape and volume), liquid (fixed volume, shape of container), gas (no fixed shape or volume).
flashcards.front: Name the three states of matter and one property of each.

flashcards.back: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Jupiter is the largest; Mercury is the smallest and closest to the Sun.
flashcards.front: List the eight planets in order from the Sun.

flashcards.back: Renewable: solar, wind, hydropower. Non-renewable: coal, oil, natural gas.
flashcards.front: Sort these into renewable and non-renewable: solar, wind, coal, oil, hydropower, natural gas.

flashcards.back: Word is for writing documents (.docx); Excel is for numbers and formulas (.xlsx); PowerPoint is for slide presentations (.pptx).
flashcards.front: What is each MS Office program used for: Word, Excel, PowerPoint?

flashcards.back: =SUM(A1:A5) adds cells A1 to A5. Formulas start with '='; B5 means column B, row 5.
flashcards.front: In Excel, what does =SUM(A1:A5) do, and what does the address B5 mean?

flashcards.back: CPU — the processor, the brain of the computer. RAM — short-term memory, cleared when the computer turns off.
flashcards.front: What do CPU and RAM do in a computer?

flashcards.back: Keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone (input). Monitor, printer, speakers (output).
flashcards.front: Sort these into input and output devices: keyboard, mouse, monitor, printer, scanner, speakers.

flashcards.back: A browser (e.g. Chrome) displays web pages; a search engine (e.g. Google) finds them. WWW is the system of web pages; https means a secure connection.
flashcards.front: What is the difference between a browser and a search engine?

flashcards.back: Ctrl + C copy, Ctrl + V paste, Ctrl + X cut, Ctrl + Z undo, Ctrl + S save, Ctrl + P print, Alt + Tab switch windows.
flashcards.front: What do these shortcuts do: Ctrl + C, Ctrl + V, Ctrl + X, Ctrl + Z, Ctrl + S, Ctrl + P, Alt + Tab?

flashcards.back: Pakistan — Islamabad; India — New Delhi; China — Beijing; Afghanistan — Kabul; Iran — Tehran; Australia — Canberra.
flashcards.front: Name the capitals of Pakistan, India, China, Afghanistan, Iran and Australia.

flashcards.back: Founded 1945, headquarters in New York, 193 member states; Pakistan joined in 1947.
flashcards.front: When was the UN founded, where is its headquarters, and how many members does it have?

flashcards.back: OIC — Jeddah, 57 members. SAARC — Kathmandu, 8 members. ECO — Tehran, 10 members.
flashcards.front: Match OIC, SAARC and ECO to their headquarters and number of members.

flashcards.back: Tarbela Dam — Indus River. Mangla Dam — Jhelum River. Warsak Dam — Kabul River.
flashcards.front: Match these dams to their rivers: Tarbela, Mangla, Warsak.

flashcards.back: The Indus, plus its five eastern tributaries: Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej.
flashcards.front: Name the longest river of Pakistan and its five eastern tributaries.

flashcards.back: National animal — Markhor; national bird — Chukar; national flower — Jasmine; national language — Urdu; national sport — field hockey.
flashcards.front: Name Pakistan's national animal, bird, flower, language and sport.
